# How to use this guide

Pathology II and Genetics (PATH(II)210) is a fourth-semester subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum. It has two parts:

1. **Pathology II** — special pathology of the kidneys, genital systems (male and female), breast, and central nervous system; and clinical pathology (examination of body fluids, semen, urine, and faeces). This completes the pathology started in Pathology I (Semester 3).
2. **Genetics** — a full module covering chromosomes and inheritance, teratogenesis, cancer genetics, prenatal diagnosis, genetic testing, and genetic counselling.

Together with the Pharmacology II (PHAR(II)205) paper, this subject is examined in one combined 75-mark paper at the end of Semester 4.

---

## The combined Semester 4 examination

PATH(II)210 does **not** have a separate university paper. It is examined as two sections of a **combined 3-hour, 75-mark** paper:

| Section | Subject | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Applied Pharmacology II | 38 |
| B | Pathology (Pathology I + Pathology II combined) | 25 |
| C | Genetics | 12 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

The pathology section (Section B) is **25 marks** and covers both Pathology I (Semester 3) and Pathology II (this subject). There is typically no internal choice in Section B.

The genetics section (Section C) is **12 marks** — a focused module that is worth learning thoroughly because the questions are specific and factual. There is typically no internal choice in Section C.

Confirm the exact paper pattern with your university — different universities implement the INC Regulations 2020 (Appendix 3) slightly differently.

---

## How the units are arranged

The INC Pathology II + Genetics syllabus is covered in eight unit files:

| Notes file | Content covered | INC section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | Special pathology: kidneys and urinary tract | Pathology II |
| Unit 2 | Special pathology: male and female genital systems | Pathology II |
| Unit 3 | Special pathology: breast and central nervous system | Pathology II |
| Unit 4 | Clinical pathology: body cavity fluids, semen, urine and faeces | Pathology II |
| Unit 5 | Genetics: chromosomes, karyotype, numerical and structural abnormalities, Mendelian inheritance | Genetics |
| Unit 6 | Genetics: multifactorial disease, teratogenesis, TORCH, imprinting, repeat expansions, cancer genetics, epigenetics | Genetics |
| Unit 7 | Genetics: newborn screening, prenatal diagnosis, genetic conditions in childhood and adulthood | Genetics |
| Unit 8 | Genetics: genetic services in India, genetic counselling, ethical and legal issues, nurse's role | Genetics |

The earlier Pathology I pack (Semester 3, PATH-I 210) covers Units 1–8 of that semester. For the Section B exam, revise both packs together.

---

## Practice paper pattern

### Section B (Pathology — 25 marks)

| Part | Questions | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 4 MCQs | 4 × 1 = 4 |
| Short answer | 3 short answers | 3 × 5 = 15 |
| Very short | 3 very short answers | 3 × 2 = 6 |
| **Total** | | **25** |

There is no long essay in the pathology section (long essays fall in Section A — Pharmacology).

### Section C (Genetics — 12 marks)

| Part | Questions | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 2 MCQs | 2 × 1 = 2 |
| Short answer | 1 short answer | 1 × 5 = 5 |
| Very short | 1–2 very short answers | 2 × 2 = 4 or 1 × 2 = 2 (varies) |
| Approximate total | | ~12 |

A **Quick MCQ test (20 questions, 20 minutes)** in the full pack lets you drill facts fast before a class test.

---

## Probability ratings

- **High** — comes up in most papers in some form; learn the full structured answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers, or as part of a larger question.
- **Low** — worth knowing for MCQs and very short answers.

These are estimates based on the weight of each topic in the INC syllabus and the typical style of nursing pathology and genetics papers.

---

## High-probability topics by unit

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 (Kidneys) | Nephritic vs nephrotic syndrome comparison; acute glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal); nephrotic syndrome causes; AKI vs CKD; Wilms tumour; renal cell carcinoma |
| 2 (Genital) | Cervical carcinoma (CIN, HPV, Pap smear, staging, prevention); endometrial carcinoma (PMB); ovarian tumour types; prostate carcinoma (PSA, Gleason, bone metastasis) |
| 3 (Breast and CNS) | Breast carcinoma (risk factors, receptors, treatment, nurse's role in BSE and post-mastectomy care); raised ICP signs and management; meningitis CSF comparison (bacterial vs viral vs TB) |
| 4 (Clinical pathology) | Transudate vs exudate; CSF findings table; urine casts and their significance; urinalysis interpretation; semen analysis collection |
| 5 (Chromosomes) | Down, Edwards, Patau, Turner, Klinefelter — chromosome number and features; Mendelian inheritance patterns and pedigree features; AD/AR/XLR comparisons |
| 6 (Teratogens, cancer genetics) | Critical period for teratogenesis; thalidomide, rubella, alcohol, valproate defects; TORCH infections and foetal effects; cancer genetics (TSGs, two-hit, Philadelphia chromosome) |
| 7 (Testing) | Newborn screening — conditions, timing, nurse's role in heel prick; amniocentesis vs CVS; Down syndrome features and nursing care; CF diagnosis (sweat test) and management |
| 8 (Counselling) | Pedigree symbols (draw from memory); definition and principles of genetic counselling (non-directive, process); PCPNDT Act; nurse's role at each stage; genetic red flags |

---

## Scoring tips

1. **Pathology answers:** Use cause → mechanism → morphology → features → nursing. This frame works for every disease question.
2. **Comparisons are easy marks:** Nephritic vs nephrotic, AKI vs CKD, transudate vs exudate, CSF in different types of meningitis, benign vs malignant tumour — answer these as tables.
3. **Know normal values:** Normal CSF (protein 15–45, glucose 50–80, <5 cells), normal urine (SG 1.001–1.035, protein negative, glucose negative), semen (count ≥16 million/mL, progressive motility ≥30%).
4. **Genetics questions reward exact terminology:** Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive — state the pattern name and give one clinical example.
5. **Draw the pedigree correctly when asked:** Use standard symbols; mark the proband with an arrow; a 3-generation pedigree earns marks.
6. **For very short answers (2 marks):** One definition + one example. Do not write a paragraph.
7. **Add nursing points:** Even in a pathology question, one or two nursing relevance lines lift the answer.
8. **Genetics counselling:** Always emphasise **non-directive** counselling and the patient's right to decide.
9. **Night before:** Read the "Remember" boxes at the end of each unit; run the Quick MCQ test; re-draw the CSF comparison table, nephritic vs nephrotic table, and pedigree symbols from memory.

# Last-night revision sheet

PATH(II)210 is examined in Semester 4 as **Section B (Pathology, 25 marks) + Section C (Genetics, 12 marks)** of the combined paper with Pharmacology II. If you have one hour, work through the tables below, then re-draw the pedigree symbols and the CSF comparison from memory.

---

## Pathology: must-know comparisons

**Nephritic vs nephrotic syndrome**

| Feature | Nephritic | Nephrotic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proteinuria | Mild | Massive (>3.5 g/day) |
| Haematuria | Prominent (smoky urine) | Absent or mild |
| Oedema | Periorbital, moderate | Generalised, severe |
| Hypertension | Yes | May be present |
| Serum albumin | Near normal | Very low |
| Serum lipids | Normal | High |
| Classic cause | Post-streptococcal GN | Minimal change (children), membranous GN (adults) |

**Acute kidney injury (AKI) vs chronic kidney disease (CKD)**

| Feature | AKI | CKD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Days to weeks | Months to years |
| Kidney size | Normal or enlarged | Shrunken, small |
| Anaemia | Mild or absent | Severe (↓ erythropoietin) |
| Bone disease | Absent | Renal osteodystrophy |
| Reversibility | Usually reversible | Irreversible |
| Casts | Granular (ATN), RBC (GN) | Waxy, broad casts |

---

## Body cavity fluids

**Transudate vs exudate**

| Feature | Transudate | Exudate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specific gravity | <1.012 | >1.020 |
| Protein | <3 g/dL | >3 g/dL |
| Appearance | Clear | Cloudy |
| Causes | Heart failure, nephrotic, cirrhosis | Infection, TB, malignancy, pancreatitis |

**Light's criteria:** Exudate if any one: (1) Fluid/serum protein ratio >0.5; (2) Fluid/serum LDH ratio >0.6; (3) Fluid LDH > ⅔ upper normal serum LDH.

**SAAG (ascites):** ≥1.1 g/dL → portal hypertension (cirrhosis); <1.1 g/dL → TB, malignancy.

---

## CSF comparison — the most-asked genetics/pathology table

| Parameter | Normal | Bacterial meningitis | Viral meningitis | TB meningitis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance | Clear | Turbid/purulent | Clear | Clear/xanthochromic |
| Pressure | 70–180 mmH₂O | Raised | Normal or mildly raised | Raised |
| Cells | <5 lymphocytes | Hundreds–thousands (neutrophils) | Tens–hundreds (lymphocytes) | Tens–hundreds (lymphocytes) |
| Protein | 15–45 mg/dL | High (>100) | Mildly raised | Very high (>200) |
| Glucose | 50–80 mg/dL (≥60% blood) | Very low (<40) | Normal or mildly low | Very low |
| Other | — | Gram stain/culture +ve | PCR for virus | AFB smear; ADA raised; fibrin web |

---

## Urinalysis normal values and cast significance

| Parameter | Normal |
| --- | --- |
| Specific gravity (SG) | 1.001–1.035 |
| pH | 4.5–8.0 |
| Protein | Negative (trace allowed) |
| Glucose | Negative |
| RBCs | 0–2/HPF |
| WBCs | 0–5/HPF |

| Cast type | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| Hyaline | Normal in small numbers; dehydration, exercise |
| Granular | ATN, glomerulonephritis |
| RBC casts | Glomerulonephritis (pathognomonic) |
| WBC casts | Pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis |
| Fatty casts / oval fat bodies | Nephrotic syndrome |
| Waxy / broad casts | Advanced CKD |

---

## Chromosomal syndromes — quick reference

| Syndrome | Chromosome | Key feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Down | Trisomy 21 | Intellectual disability, flat face, AV septal defect, Alzheimer's |
| Edwards | Trisomy 18 | Severe ID, rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists; die in infancy |
| Patau | Trisomy 13 | Severe ID, holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, cleft lip; die in weeks |
| Turner | 45,X | Short stature, webbed neck, amenorrhoea, coarctation; intelligence normal |
| Klinefelter | 47,XXY | Tall, azoospermia, gynaecomastia; testosterone replacement |
| Cri-du-chat | 5p deletion | Cat-like cry; intellectual disability |

---

## Mendelian inheritance — comparison

| Pattern | % risk per child | Sex affected | Parent status | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Autosomal dominant (AD) | 50% | M and F equally | One parent affected | Huntington, Marfan, NF1 |
| Autosomal recessive (AR) | 25% affected | M and F equally | Both parents carriers | CF, sickle cell, PKU, thalassaemia |
| X-linked recessive (XLR) | 50% of sons | Males predominantly | Carrier mother | Haemophilia A, DMD, G6PD deficiency |
| Mitochondrial | All children of affected mother | M and F (from mother only) | Mother affected | MELAS, MERRF, LHON |

---

## Key teratogens and defects

| Teratogen | Main defect |
| --- | --- |
| Thalidomide | Phocomelia (limb defects), ear defects |
| Rubella (1st trimester) | Cataracts, deafness, PDA (congenital rubella syndrome) |
| Alcohol | FASD (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, intellectual disability) |
| Valproic acid | Neural tube defects (20× increased risk) |
| Isotretinoin | CNS defects, ear/face defects, cardiac defects |
| Warfarin | Warfarin embryopathy (1st trimester), CNS haemorrhage (2nd/3rd) |

---

## TORCH infections and foetal effects

| Infection | Key foetal/neonatal effect |
| --- | --- |
| Toxoplasma gondii | Chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus |
| Rubella | Cataracts, deafness, PDA |
| Cytomegalovirus (CMV) | Periventricular calcifications, hearing loss; most common intrauterine infection |
| Herpes simplex (HSV) | Neonatal herpes — vesicles, encephalitis; treat with IV aciclovir |
| Syphilis | Saddle nose, Hutchinson's teeth, periostitis |

---

## Cancer genetics

| Gene / mechanism | Syndrome / cancer |
| --- | --- |
| TP53 (TSG) | Li-Fraumeni syndrome; most commonly mutated gene in cancer |
| BRCA1 / BRCA2 (TSG) | Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer |
| APC (TSG) | Familial adenomatous polyposis → colorectal cancer |
| RB1 (TSG) | Retinoblastoma (prototype two-hit model) |
| KRAS (oncogene) | Pancreatic (95%), colorectal, lung cancer |
| BCR-ABL, t(9;22) | Philadelphia chromosome → CML; treated with imatinib |
| MYC, t(8;14) | Burkitt lymphoma |

**Knudson's two-hit hypothesis:** TSG cancer requires mutation of both alleles; in hereditary cancer, the first hit is inherited in every cell, so the second somatic hit is enough to cause cancer (earlier onset).

---

## Pedigree symbols (draw from memory)

```text
 □  Unaffected male         ■  Affected male
 ○  Unaffected female       ●  Affected female
 □─○  Mating couple
  │   Line of descent
 □═○  Consanguineous couple (double horizontal line)
 □ with /  Deceased
 ◔  Carrier female (XLR)
Arrow →  points to the proband (index case)
Siblings: drawn left to right, oldest first, on a horizontal sibship line
```

---

## Genetic counselling — key points

- **Non-directive:** Counsellor presents facts; client makes their own decision.
- **Process:** Multiple sessions; not a single event.
- **Steps:** Confirm diagnosis → draw pedigree → calculate risk → discuss options → support decision.
- **PCPNDT Act (India):** Foetal sex determination for sex selection is illegal; mandatory registration of prenatal diagnostic centres.
- **MTP Act (amended 2021):** Termination up to 24 weeks (specific categories); no upper limit for foetal conditions incompatible with life (medical board required).
- **Right not to know:** Must be respected for predictive testing (Huntington's, BRCA).

---

## Exam reminder

PATH(II)210 is examined with Pharmacology II in Semester 4. This paper carries **37 marks** for Pathology + Genetics (B + C combined). Revision of **Pathology I** (Semester 3 notes pack) is also needed for Section B — that pack covers general pathology, inflammation, neoplasia, circulatory disturbances, and systemic pathology of the respiratory, cardiovascular, GIT, liver, skeletal, endocrine systems, and haematological tests. Treat the two packs as one body of knowledge for Section B.

# Unit 1: Special pathology — kidneys and urinary tract

This unit covers INC Unit I of Pathology II: diseases of the kidneys and urinary tract. Learn each disease as cause → mechanism → morphological changes → clinical and laboratory features → nursing relevance.

---

## 1.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

Each kidney contains about one million **nephrons** — the filtering units. Each nephron has a glomerulus (a tuft of capillaries enclosed in Bowman's capsule) where filtration happens, then a tubule that modifies the filtrate (reabsorption and secretion) to produce urine.

```text
Kidney structure (simplified)
Renal artery → afferent arteriole → glomerulus (filtration)
→ Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → Loop of Henle
→ distal tubule → collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder
```

| Normal kidney function | Reference value |
| --- | --- |
| Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) | ~125 mL/min (60–120 mL/min is accepted) |
| Serum creatinine | 0.6–1.2 mg/dL (men), 0.5–1.0 mg/dL (women) |
| Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) | 7–20 mg/dL |
| Urine output | ~1–2 L/day (minimum 400 mL/day) |

The urinary tract below the kidneys: two **ureters** carry urine to the **urinary bladder**, which stores urine until voiding through the **urethra**.

---

## 1.2 Glomerular diseases

### Acute glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal)

- **Cause:** Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus infection (throat or skin) 1–3 weeks before. Immune complexes (antigen-antibody) deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and activate complement.
- **Mechanism:** Immune-complex deposition → complement activation → neutrophil and monocyte infiltration → hypercellularity of glomeruli → reduced filtration area.
- **Morphology:** Diffuse hypercellularity of glomeruli on biopsy; granular ("lumpy-bumpy") deposits of IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence.
- **Features (nephritic syndrome):**
  - Haematuria — dark, smoky, tea-coloured or frank red urine (blood in urine)
  - Proteinuria — mild (not massive)
  - Oedema — periorbital (puffy face, especially in the morning) and ankle oedema
  - Oliguria — reduced urine output
  - Hypertension — from salt and water retention
  - Raised anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titre — confirms recent streptococcal infection
- **Outcome:** Most children recover fully; some adults develop chronic GN.
- **Nursing:** Bed rest in acute phase; strict input-output chart; daily weight to track fluid; low-salt diet; antihypertensives as ordered; antibiotics to eradicate residual streptococcal infection; urine dipstick to track haematuria.

### Nephrotic syndrome

Defined as: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria. The common causes are:

| Cause | Age group | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal change disease | Children (most common in children) | Podocyte foot process effacement only on electron microscopy; excellent steroid response |
| Membranous nephropathy | Adults | Subepithelial deposits; idiopathic or secondary to diabetes, SLE, hepatitis B, drugs |
| Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis | Any age | Secondary to hypertension, obesity, HIV; poor prognosis |
| Diabetic nephropathy | Adults | Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules on biopsy; most common cause of end-stage renal disease |

- **Mechanism:** Loss of glomerular basement membrane negative charge or structural damage → massive leakage of albumin → hypoalbuminaemia → low oncotic pressure → water and salt leak into tissues (oedema).
- **Features:**
  - Oedema — generalised (face, legs, abdomen), pitting, worse in the morning
  - Frothy urine (proteinuria)
  - Ascites and pleural effusion in severe cases
  - Hyperlipidaemia — the liver makes more lipoprotein to compensate for lost albumin
  - Lipiduria — fat globules and oval fat bodies in urine
  - Increased risk of infection (immunoglobulins lost in urine) and thrombosis (clotting factors lost)

**Comparison: nephritic vs nephrotic syndrome**

| Feature | Nephritic syndrome | Nephrotic syndrome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proteinuria | Mild | Massive (>3.5 g/day) |
| Haematuria | Prominent | Absent or mild |
| Oedema | Moderate | Severe, generalised |
| Hypertension | Yes | May be present |
| Serum albumin | Near normal | Markedly low |
| Serum lipids | Normal | High (hyperlipidaemia) |
| Typical cause | Post-streptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy | Minimal change, membranous GN, diabetic nephropathy |

- **Nursing:** Keep accurate fluid and weight records; skin care for pitting oedema (elevate legs, prevent pressure sores); low-sodium diet; treat infection early; explain steroid therapy (do not stop suddenly, monitor blood sugar and BP).

### IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease)

- Most common glomerulonephritis worldwide.
- IgA deposits in the mesangium.
- Presents with **recurrent episodes of frank haematuria** after upper respiratory tract infections or exercise.
- Typically benign in children; some adults progress slowly to renal failure.

---

## 1.3 Tubular diseases

### Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

- Most common cause of **acute kidney injury** (AKI).
- Two types:
  - **Ischaemic ATN:** from prolonged hypotension (shock, major surgery, haemorrhage); inner medulla (thick ascending limb and straight segment of proximal tubule) is most vulnerable.
  - **Toxic ATN:** from nephrotoxins — aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin), contrast dye, myoglobin (from rhabdomyolysis), haemoglobin (from haemolysis), heavy metals, organic solvents.
- **Morphology:** Tubular epithelial cell necrosis with flattening and loss of brush border; tubular casts in distal tubules.
- **Features:** Sudden rise in creatinine and BUN; oliguria or anuria; hyperkalaemia; metabolic acidosis; volume overload.
- **Recovery:** Most cases are reversible with time; during the recovery phase urine output increases dramatically (polyuria phase) — watch for hypokalaemia.
- **Nursing:** Strict fluid balance; daily weight; nephrotoxic drugs avoided; dietary protein restriction; dialysis if severe.

### Fanconi syndrome

- Generalised proximal tubule dysfunction → inability to reabsorb glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid.
- Causes: Wilson's disease, cystinosis, multiple myeloma, heavy metal poisoning, drugs (tenofovir, valproate).
- Features: glycosuria with normal blood sugar, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, rickets/osteomalacia.

---

## 1.4 Renal vascular disease

- **Hypertensive nephrosclerosis:** Long-standing hypertension → thickening of afferent arteriole walls (hyaline arteriolosclerosis) → reduction of glomerular blood supply → glomerulosclerosis and tubular atrophy. Kidneys become small and granular ("granular contracted kidney").
- **Renal artery stenosis:** Usually from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia → reduced renal perfusion → renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation → secondary hypertension (renovascular hypertension). Treat with angioplasty or surgery.

---

## 1.5 Interstitial nephritis

- Inflammation of the renal interstitium (not primarily glomeruli or tubules).
- **Acute interstitial nephritis:** Most often a drug hypersensitivity reaction (NSAIDs, penicillin, sulphonamides, diuretics) — fever, skin rash, eosinophilia and rising creatinine within weeks of starting the drug. Withdraw the offending drug; steroids hasten recovery.
- **Chronic interstitial nephritis:** From analgesic nephropathy (long-term NSAID use), reflux nephropathy (vesico-ureteric reflux with recurrent pyelonephritis), lead or cadmium poisoning, or myeloma. Leads slowly to chronic kidney disease.

---

## 1.6 Renal failure

### Acute kidney injury (AKI)

- Rapid rise in blood creatinine and urea over hours to days.
- Causes classified as: pre-renal (hypovolaemia, heart failure — most common, 60%), intrinsic renal (ATN, GN, interstitial nephritis), post-renal (obstruction — stones, BPH, tumour).
- Features: oliguria/anuria, rising creatinine and urea, hyperkalaemia (risk of cardiac arrest), metabolic acidosis, oedema, confusion.
- **Reversible** if the cause is treated quickly.

### Chronic kidney disease (CKD)

- Gradual, irreversible loss of nephrons over months to years.
- Causes: diabetic nephropathy (most common in India), hypertensive nephrosclerosis, chronic GN, reflux nephropathy.
- Staged GFR 1–5; stage 5 (GFR <15) = end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis or transplant.
- Features: anaemia (↓ erythropoietin), hypertension, bone disease (↓ vitamin D), uraemia (nausea, vomiting, pruritus, encephalopathy), pericarditis, peripheral neuropathy.

**Comparison: AKI vs CKD**

| Feature | AKI | CKD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Days to weeks | Months to years |
| Kidney size | Normal or enlarged | Reduced, shrunken |
| Anaemia | Mild or absent | Severe (normochromic normocytic) |
| Bone disease | Absent | Present (renal osteodystrophy) |
| Reversibility | Often reversible | Irreversible |
| Urinalysis | Granular casts (ATN), RBC casts (GN) | Waxy, broad casts |

**Nursing care in renal failure:**
- Accurate input-output record; daily weight.
- Restrict fluid (input = output + insensible losses).
- Low-potassium and low-phosphate diet; moderate protein restriction.
- Monitor ECG for hyperkalaemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS).
- Prepare patient for dialysis (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) as ordered.
- Fistula care for haemodialysis patients (no BP cuff or venepuncture on the fistula arm).
- Psychosocial support; education about diet, fluid restriction, and medications.

---

## 1.7 Renal tumours

### Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)

- Most common **abdominal tumour in children** (peak age 3–4 years).
- Arises from embryonal renal tissue; associated with WT1 gene mutation.
- **Features:** Smooth, large abdominal mass (often the parent notices it while bathing the child), haematuria, hypertension, fever.
- **Morphology:** Triphasic tumour — blastema, stromal, and epithelial elements.
- **Treatment:** Surgery (nephrectomy) + chemotherapy ± radiotherapy; prognosis is good.
- **Nursing:** Do not palpate the abdomen repeatedly (can rupture the capsule and seed tumour cells); prepare child and family for surgery and chemotherapy; handle the child gently; support the family emotionally.

### Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)

- Most common renal malignancy in adults; peak age 50–70 years.
- Arises from renal tubular epithelium; clear cell type is most common.
- **Risk factors:** Smoking (doubles risk), obesity, hypertension, von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
- **Classic triad:** Haematuria + flank pain + flank mass (less than one-third have all three today; often found incidentally on ultrasound).
- **Paraneoplastic syndromes:** Polycythaemia (erythropoietin production), hypercalcaemia (PTHrP), Cushing's syndrome, hypertension.
- **Metastases:** Lung (cannon-ball deposits), bone, liver, brain — through blood.
- **Treatment:** Partial or radical nephrectomy; targeted therapy (sunitinib) for advanced disease; RCC is resistant to chemotherapy.
- **Nursing:** Prepare for nephrectomy; post-operative wound and drain care; monitor for bleeding; educate on smoking cessation.

### Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder

- Most common malignancy of the urinary tract.
- **Risk factors:** Cigarette smoking (most important), occupational exposure to aniline dyes (rubber, textile, leather industries), cyclophosphamide, schistosomiasis (squamous cell type in Africa).
- **Features:** Painless haematuria (most common presenting symptom), frequency and dysuria, urinary obstruction.
- **Diagnosis:** Cystoscopy with biopsy (gold standard); urine cytology.
- **Treatment:** Transurethral resection (TURBT) for superficial; radical cystectomy + chemotherapy for muscle-invasive; intravesical BCG for high-grade superficial.
- **Nursing:** Educate on haematuria — any painless haematuria must be investigated; catheter care post-cystoscopy; post-cystectomy stoma care (urostomy or ileal conduit); smoking cessation counselling.

---

## Remember

- Nephritic syndrome: haematuria + mild proteinuria + hypertension + oliguria; post-streptococcal GN is the classic cause; check ASO titre.
- Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → generalised oedema + hyperlipidaemia; minimal change disease is the most common cause in children.
- ATN is the most common cause of AKI; ischaemic (from shock) or toxic (aminoglycosides, contrast); usually reversible.
- CKD = small kidneys, severe anaemia, bone disease, uraemia — not reversible; stage by GFR.
- Wilms tumour: children, large abdominal mass — do not palpate aggressively; treat with surgery + chemotherapy.
- RCC: adults, haematuria + flank pain + mass; spreads via blood; smoking is the main risk; treatment is surgery.
- Bladder TCC: painless haematuria; smoking and dye industry exposure are key risks; diagnosed by cystoscopy.

# Unit 2: Special pathology — male and female genital systems

This unit covers diseases of the male and female reproductive tracts — tumours, inflammatory conditions, and premalignant lesions. Learn each as cause → morphology → features → treatment → nurse's role.

---

## PART A — MALE GENITAL SYSTEM

## 2.1 Testicular tumours

The testis produces two main tumour categories: **germ cell tumours** (95% — derived from spermatogenic cells) and sex-cord stromal tumours.

### Seminoma

- Most common testicular germ cell tumour; peak age 25–45 years.
- **Morphology:** Homogeneous, pale grey-white cut surface; large uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei; lymphocytic infiltrate.
- **Tumour markers:** β-HCG mildly raised in a minority; AFP is **not** raised (a seminoma that raises AFP is actually a non-seminomatous component).
- **Features:** Painless, smooth enlargement of one testis; retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis; lung metastasis in advanced disease.
- **Treatment:** Orchidectomy via inguinal approach (not scrotal — avoids scrotal lymphatic seeding) + radiotherapy ± chemotherapy; excellent cure rate.

### Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT)

Includes embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour (most common in infants — AFP raised), choriocarcinoma (β-HCG raised, most aggressive, haematogenous spread early), and teratoma (contains mature tissue from all three germ layers — may have teeth, hair, cartilage; mature teratoma is benign in children, malignant in adults).

| Tumour marker | Useful in |
| --- | --- |
| AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) | Yolk sac tumour, mixed NSGCT — not raised in pure seminoma |
| β-HCG (beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin) | Choriocarcinoma, some seminomas |
| LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) | Bulk marker of disease |

Markers guide treatment response and detect recurrence.

## 2.2 Cryptorchidism

- Undescended testis (retained in the abdomen or inguinal canal).
- Risk of **malignancy is 4–10× higher** than in a normally descended testis; contralateral normally descended testis risk is also slightly elevated, suggesting a systemic predisposition.
- Also causes infertility if bilateral (high temperature impairs spermatogenesis).
- **Management:** Orchidopexy (surgical fixation in the scrotum) ideally before age 2 years to reduce malignancy risk and preserve fertility.

## 2.3 Epididymo-orchitis

- Acute infection of the epididymis and testis.
- In young sexually active men: **Chlamydia trachomatis** and **Neisseria gonorrhoeae**.
- In older men and children: **E. coli** and other Gram-negative bacilli (associated with urinary tract infection or structural abnormality).
- Features: Painful, tender, hot, swollen scrotum; fever; dysuria.
- Distinguish from torsion of testis (torsion is an emergency with sudden onset, no fever, negative Prehn's sign — lifting does not relieve pain — requires immediate surgery).
- **Treatment:** Antibiotics based on cause; scrotal support; analgesia.

## 2.4 Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

- Very common in men over 50; nearly universal by 80 years.
- Affects the **periurethral (transition zone)** of the prostate — compresses the urethra.
- **Morphology:** Nodular hyperplasia of glands and stroma; not a cancer, does not become cancer.
- **Features:**
  - Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS): hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, sensation of incomplete emptying (obstructive); frequency, urgency, nocturia (irritative).
  - Acute urinary retention is an emergency needing immediate catheterisation.
  - Chronic retention → back pressure on kidneys → hydronephrosis → renal failure.
- **Diagnosis:** PSA (mildly elevated in BPH; much higher in cancer), uroflowmetry, ultrasound residual urine.
- **Treatment:** Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin — relax smooth muscle), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride — shrink gland), transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) for severe cases.
- **Nursing:** Pre-TURP: explain procedure, bowel preparation; Post-TURP: continuous bladder irrigation (watch for clots blocking the catheter, TUR syndrome — hyponatraemia from fluid absorption), measure urine colour and output; catheter care; teach that some haematuria is expected initially; explain that TURP can cause retrograde ejaculation.

## 2.5 Carcinoma of the prostate

- Most common cancer in men in the West; increasing in India.
- Arises from the **peripheral zone** of the prostate — does not cause urinary obstruction early (unlike BPH which is in the periurethral zone).
- **Risk factors:** Age (most common after 65), family history, Black African descent.
- **Morphology:** Adenocarcinoma; Gleason grading system (5 patterns of gland differentiation, two most prominent areas scored 1–5 each; Gleason score 2–10; score ≥7 = high grade, aggressive).
- **Features:** Often asymptomatic; found by raised PSA on screening. When locally advanced: LUTS, haematuria, haemospermia. When metastatic: bone pain from **osteoblastic** (bone-forming) metastases — in lumbar spine, pelvis, femur (high alkaline phosphatase and PSA).
- **Diagnosis:** PSA + digital rectal examination (DRE) → transrectal ultrasound biopsy.
- **Treatment:**
  - Localised: active surveillance, radical prostatectomy, or radiotherapy.
  - Advanced: androgen deprivation therapy (castration — surgical or chemical with LHRH agonists), abiraterone, chemotherapy.
- **Nursing:** PSA counselling; pre-operative bowel preparation; post-prostatectomy: catheter care, pelvic floor exercises for urinary incontinence; emotional support (erectile dysfunction and incontinence affect quality of life); teach bone metastasis warning signs (new back pain).

---

## PART B — FEMALE GENITAL SYSTEM

## 2.6 Cervical pathology

### Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN)

- CIN is **premalignant** dysplasia of the squamocolumnar junction (transformation zone) of the cervix.
- **Cause:** Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection — types **16 and 18** are responsible for about 70% of cervical cancers.

| Grade | Dysplasia extent | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CIN 1 | Lower ⅓ of epithelium | Most regress spontaneously |
| CIN 2 | Lower ⅔ | Intermediate risk |
| CIN 3 | Full-thickness (carcinoma in situ) | High risk of progression if untreated |

- **Diagnosis:** Pap (Papanicolaou) smear → colposcopy and biopsy.
- **Treatment:** CIN 1: observe; CIN 2–3: ablation (cryotherapy, laser) or excision (LLETZ/cone biopsy).
- **Prevention:** HPV vaccination (girls 9–14 years — most effective before first exposure); regular Pap smear screening.

### Cervical carcinoma

- Most common gynaecological cancer in India and many low-income countries.
- **Squamous cell carcinoma** (80%); adenocarcinoma (20% — from endocervical glands).
- **Risk factors:** HPV 16/18, multiple sexual partners, early first sexual intercourse, immunosuppression, smoking, lack of screening.
- **Features:** Irregular vaginal bleeding (especially post-coital), offensive vaginal discharge, pelvic pain in advanced disease.
- **Staging (FIGO):**
  - Stage I: confined to cervix.
  - Stage II: extends beyond uterus but not to pelvic wall or lower vagina.
  - Stage III: reaches pelvic wall or lower vagina or causes hydronephrosis.
  - Stage IV: beyond true pelvis or involves bladder/rectum.
- **Treatment:** Early (I–IIA): surgery (Wertheim's hysterectomy) or RT; advanced: concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin + RT).
- **Nurse's role in prevention:** Educate women on HPV vaccination; promote Pap smear uptake (especially for women 21–65 years); reduce stigma; explain that early-stage disease is curable; support women during RT (perineal skin care, diarrhoea management, fatigue, emotional support).

## 2.7 Endometrial pathology

### Endometrial hyperplasia

- Excess oestrogen stimulation without progesterone opposition → glandular overgrowth.
- Risk factors: obesity (peripheral oestrogen from fat), polycystic ovary syndrome, unopposed oestrogen therapy, oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumour.
- **Simple hyperplasia without atypia:** low cancer risk; treat with progestogens.
- **Atypical hyperplasia:** significant cancer risk; hysterectomy recommended.

### Endometrial carcinoma

- Most common gynaecological cancer in Western countries; second in India.
- **Type I (most common):** Endometrioid adenocarcinoma; linked to excess oestrogen; presents early (stage I); good prognosis.
- **Type II:** Serous or clear cell; not oestrogen-driven; aggressive; worse prognosis.
- **Features:** Post-menopausal bleeding (PMB) — any PMB must be investigated until cancer is excluded. In pre-menopausal women: irregular heavy bleeding.
- **Diagnosis:** Transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial thickness) → endometrial biopsy.
- **Treatment:** Total abdominal hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy ± radiotherapy; progestogen therapy for early-stage in women who want fertility.

## 2.8 Ovarian tumours

Ovarian tumours are the most common cause of death from gynaecological cancer in Western countries because they are often silent until late.

**Broad classification:**

| Group | Main types | Tumour markers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surface epithelial (most common — 65%) | Serous cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma, mucinous cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma, endometrioid | CA-125 (serous), CEA (mucinous) |
| Germ cell (more common in young women) | Dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma — benign, most common in young women), dysgerminoma (malignant), yolk sac tumour | AFP (yolk sac), β-HCG (choriocarcinoma) |
| Sex cord-stromal | Granulosa cell tumour (oestrogen-secreting → precocious puberty in girls, PMB in women), thecoma, fibroma, Sertoli-Leydig | Inhibin (granulosa cell) |
| Metastatic (Krukenberg tumour) | Bilateral metastasis from stomach, colon or breast | Varies with primary |

- **Dermoid cyst (mature teratoma):** Most common benign ovarian cyst in reproductive age; contains teeth, hair, sebaceous material; benign but can tort (twist), causing sudden severe pelvic pain.
- **Serous cystadenocarcinoma:** Most common malignant ovarian tumour; bilateral in 60%; spreads by peritoneal seeding; psammoma bodies (calcification) on microscopy; presents with abdominal distension (ascites).
- **Krukenberg tumour:** Bilateral ovarian metastases from gastric carcinoma (signet-ring cells in a fibroblastic stroma); malignant.

## 2.9 Vulval conditions

- **Lichen sclerosus:** Thin white plaques; itching and soreness; benign but slight increased risk of squamous carcinoma; treated with potent topical steroids.
- **Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN):** Premalignant dysplasia; associated with HPV 16/18; treated by excision or laser.
- **Squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva:** Older women; presents as an ulcerative or exophytic lesion; treated by wide local excision ± inguinal lymph node dissection.

## 2.10 Common inflammatory conditions

| Condition | Cause | Features | Nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) | Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, mixed anaerobes ascending from cervix | Bilateral lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, purulent discharge, fever | IV antibiotics (broad spectrum), IV fluids, pain management, contact tracing, education on STI prevention |
| Cervicitis | Chlamydia, gonorrhoea | Mucopurulent discharge; often asymptomatic | Screen and treat sexual partner; use condoms |
| Trichomonas vaginitis | Trichomonas vaginalis (STI) | Frothy greenish offensive discharge, pruritus, "strawberry cervix" | Metronidazole for patient AND partner |
| Candida vaginitis | Candida albicans | Thick white "cottage-cheese" discharge, intense pruritus; recurs with antibiotics, diabetes, immunosuppression | Topical or oral azole antifungals |
| Bacterial vaginosis (BV) | Overgrowth of anaerobes (Gardnerella vaginalis) | Thin grey discharge with fishy smell; not an STI | Metronidazole; can recur |

---

## Remember

- Testicular germ cell tumours: seminoma = radiosensitive; NSGCT = AFP/β-HCG raised depending on type. Orchidectomy via inguinal route.
- Cryptorchidism: 4–10× cancer risk; orchidopexy before age 2.
- BPH: periurethral zone, obstructive symptoms; TURP — post-op continuous irrigation, watch for TUR syndrome.
- Prostate carcinoma: peripheral zone, osteoblastic bone metastases, PSA raised; androgen deprivation therapy for metastatic.
- HPV 16/18 → CIN → cervical carcinoma; Pap smear screening + HPV vaccine prevent it.
- PMB (post-menopausal bleeding) must be investigated — endometrial carcinoma until proved otherwise.
- Ovarian cancers are silent until late; most common cause of gynaecological cancer death.
- Krukenberg tumour = bilateral ovarian metastasis from gastric carcinoma.
- PID: bilateral pelvic pain + cervical motion tenderness; treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics including anaerobic cover and trace sexual contacts.

# Unit 3: Special pathology — breast and central nervous system

This unit covers pathology of the breast (benign and malignant) and the central nervous system (oedema, infections, and tumours). Learn each condition as cause → morphology → features → management → nurse's role.

---

## PART A — BREAST

## 3.1 Anatomy revision

The breast is composed of 15–20 lobes of glandular tissue, ducts, and fatty stroma, all supported by Cooper's ligaments (which attach to the overlying skin). The upper outer quadrant contains the most tissue and is where most breast cancers arise. The main draining lymph nodes are axillary (most important — levels I, II, III).

## 3.2 Fibrocystic change

- Most common benign breast condition in women of reproductive age (25–50 years).
- Not a single disease — an umbrella term for several hormonally driven changes:
  - **Cysts:** fluid-filled cavities; fluctuate with the menstrual cycle.
  - **Fibrosis:** replacement of stroma by dense fibrous tissue.
  - **Adenosis:** increase in the number and size of acini (lobular units).
  - **Epithelial hyperplasia:** increase in ductal or lobular epithelial cells; hyperplasia without atypia — slight increase in cancer risk; atypical hyperplasia — 4–5× increased risk.
- **Features:** Bilateral, often upper outer quadrant, painful, tender nodularity that worsens before menstruation; may discharge from nipple.
- **Nursing:** Reassurance that most fibrocystic change is benign; well-fitting bra; evening primrose oil helps some; any new discrete lump or bloody nipple discharge needs further investigation.

## 3.3 Fibroadenoma

- Most common benign breast **tumour** in young women (15–35 years).
- Benign proliferation of both ductal and stromal elements.
- **Features:** Smooth, well-defined, rubbery, **mobile** ("breast mouse") lump; non-tender; size 1–3 cm; does not change with the cycle (unlike fibrocystic change, which fluctuates).
- **Management:** Ultrasound + fine-needle aspiration (triple assessment: clinical + imaging + cytology); if benign, can be observed or excised if large or symptomatic.
- **Nursing:** Reassurance that it is not cancer; explain the triple assessment; teach that any change in size warrants re-review.

## 3.4 Breast carcinoma

The most common cancer in women worldwide and the leading cause of cancer death in women in India.

### Risk factors

| Factor | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| BRCA1 / BRCA2 mutations | Lifetime risk 50–80%; also high ovarian cancer risk |
| Family history | First-degree relative doubles risk |
| Early menarche, late menopause | Prolonged oestrogen exposure |
| Nulliparity / late first pregnancy | No protective pregnancy-related changes |
| Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) | Small increased risk with combined HRT |
| Prior radiation to chest | (e.g. for Hodgkin lymphoma) |
| Obesity (post-menopausal) | Peripheral oestrogen from fat |
| Alcohol | Dose-related risk |

### Pre-invasive lesions

- **Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS):** Malignant cells fill the ducts; basement membrane intact; not yet invasive. Usually detected on mammography (microcalcifications). Treated by wide local excision ± radiotherapy.
- **Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS):** Malignant cells fill lobules; often bilateral; marker of increased risk; not treated by excision but managed by surveillance or risk-reducing surgery.

### Invasive types

| Type | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC, NOS) | Most common (75%); irregular hard mass; may tether skin or cause nipple retraction |
| Invasive lobular carcinoma | 10%; bilateral in 10–20%; "Indian file" cell pattern on microscopy; diffuse growth, may be missed on imaging |
| Medullary carcinoma | Softer, well-circumscribed; lymphocytic infiltrate; paradoxically better prognosis |
| Inflammatory carcinoma | Dermal lymphatic invasion → red, oedematous, warm skin ("peau d'orange"); aggressive; Stage IIIB |

### Staging (TNM)

- T: tumour size; N: nodal status (axillary nodes — most important prognostic factor); M: distant metastases.
- **Stage I–II:** Localised, potentially curable by surgery ± RT.
- **Stage III:** Locally advanced (skin, chest wall, matted nodes).
- **Stage IV:** Distant metastases — bone (most common), liver, lung, brain; not curable but treatable.

### Molecular subtypes and receptors

| Receptor | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| ER (oestrogen receptor) positive | Hormone therapy effective (tamoxifen for pre-menopausal, aromatase inhibitor for post-menopausal) |
| PR (progesterone receptor) positive | Also responds to hormone therapy |
| HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) over-expressed | Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is effective; more aggressive without treatment |
| Triple negative (ER−/PR−/HER2−) | No targeted therapy available; chemotherapy only; aggressive |

### Treatment

- **Surgery:** Wide local excision (lumpectomy) + radiotherapy = mastectomy in terms of survival; modified radical mastectomy (removes breast + axillary nodes); sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB — avoids full axillary clearance if no nodal metastasis).
- **Radiotherapy:** After breast-conserving surgery or for locally advanced disease.
- **Chemotherapy:** Pre-operative (neoadjuvant — shrinks tumour) or post-operative (adjuvant); regimens include anthracyclines (doxorubicin) + cyclophosphamide, taxanes.
- **Hormone therapy:** Tamoxifen (selective oestrogen receptor modulator) for pre-menopausal ER+ women; aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole) for post-menopausal ER+ women.
- **Targeted therapy:** Trastuzumab (Herceptin) for HER2+ disease.

### Nurse's role

- **Breast self-examination (BSE) teaching:** Monthly self-examination after menstruation; look (in front of a mirror — changes in shape, dimpling, nipple change) and feel (all four quadrants + axilla, in a systematic pattern). Emphasise that BSE detects changes; clinical breast examination and mammography are needed for diagnosis.
- **Screening:** Annual mammography for women ≥40 years (or earlier with family history/BRCA).
- **Post-mastectomy care:** Drain management and monitoring; arm exercises to prevent lymphoedema (start gently on day 1); no BP cuff or venepuncture on the ipsilateral arm; prevent injury, burns, infections on that arm; teach hand and arm hygiene.
- **Lymphoedema management:** Elevation, compression sleeves, gentle massage, weight management.
- **Psychological support:** Body image issues after mastectomy; prosthesis fitting and information on breast reconstruction; support groups; partner communication.
- **Chemotherapy side effects:** Nausea (antiemetics), alopecia (hair will regrow), neutropenia (infection precautions), mucositis (oral care).

---

## PART B — CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM

## 3.5 Cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure (ICP)

### Types of cerebral oedema

| Type | Mechanism | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vasogenic | Blood-brain barrier breakdown → plasma leaks into extracellular space | Tumours, abscess, contusion, haemorrhage |
| Cytotoxic | Cellular swelling (Na/K pump failure) | Ischaemia, hypoxia |
| Interstitial | CSF leaks out through ependyma | Obstructive hydrocephalus |

### Raised intracranial pressure (ICP)

- Normal ICP: 7–15 mmHg.
- **Causes:** Brain tumour, cerebral oedema, hydrocephalus, subdural or extradural haematoma, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
- **Effects:** Headache (worse in the morning and on straining), vomiting (projectile, without nausea), papilloedema (blurring of optic disc margin on fundoscopy — a critical sign), altered consciousness.
- **Herniation:** Uncal herniation (transtentorial) → compression of CN III (dilated, fixed pupil ipsilateral to the lesion) → "blown pupil" → compression of brainstem → death. **A unilateral dilated fixed pupil is a neurosurgical emergency.**
- **Cushing's triad (late sign):** Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respirations.
- **Management:** Head elevation 30°; mannitol (osmotic diuretic); dexamethasone (for tumour-related oedema); hyperventilation (↓ CO₂ → cerebral vasoconstriction); surgical decompression.
- **Nursing:** Neurological observations hourly (GCS, pupils, limb movements, vital signs); head elevated 30°; keep patient calm (stimulation raises ICP); prevent straining (stool softeners); maintain airway; report any sudden deterioration immediately.

## 3.6 Meningitis

Inflammation of the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid), usually from infection.

| Type | Common cause | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bacterial | Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (children), Listeria (neonates and elderly) | Sudden high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia; petechial or purpuric rash (meningococcal — non-blanching = emergency); CSF — turbid, high protein, very low glucose, neutrophils |
| Viral (aseptic) | Enteroviruses (most common), herpes simplex, mumps | Milder; CSF — clear, slightly raised protein, normal or mildly low glucose, lymphocytes; self-limiting in most |
| Tuberculous (TB) | Mycobacterium tuberculosis | Gradual onset; basal meningitis (cranial nerve palsies — CN VI, CN III); CSF — clear/xanthochromic, very high protein, very low glucose, lymphocytes, AFB; fibrinous exudate at base; treat with 4-drug anti-TB regimen |

**Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome:** Overwhelming meningococcal septicaemia → bilateral adrenal haemorrhage → adrenal crisis. Fulminant course with purpuric rash, DIC, hypotension; fatal without immediate treatment.

**Nursing care in meningitis:**
- Isolate bacterial meningitis (droplet precautions until 24 hours of antibiotics).
- Dim lighting, quiet environment (photophobia and phonophobia).
- IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) as an emergency — time to antibiotics is critical.
- IV dexamethasone to reduce inflammation and hearing loss.
- Monitor for complications: seizures (padded cot sides, suction ready), raised ICP, hydrocephalus, hearing loss.
- Observe petechiae progress; non-blanching rash spreading rapidly is life-threatening.
- Prophylaxis: rifampicin for household contacts of meningococcal meningitis.

## 3.7 Encephalitis

- Inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself.
- **Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE):** Most common sporadic viral encephalitis in adults; HSV-1 reactivation; involves the **temporal lobes** (and frontal lobes) → fever, headache, personality change, memory loss, aphasia, seizures; MRI shows temporal lobe signal change; treat promptly with **IV aciclovir** (delays = higher mortality/disability).
- **Japanese encephalitis:** Most common viral encephalitis in India; flavivirus transmitted by Culex mosquito; children most affected; vaccine available.
- **Nursing:** Seizure precautions; antiviral as ordered; supportive care; screen contacts for mosquito-borne encephalitis (Japanese encephalitis epidemic management).

## 3.8 Brain abscess

- Collection of pus within the brain parenchyma; surrounded by a capsule.
- **Sources:** Direct spread (mastoiditis → temporal lobe; sinusitis → frontal lobe), haematogenous (lung abscess, cyanotic heart disease, dental extraction — via right-to-left shunt), penetrating head injury.
- **Features:** Raised ICP (headache, vomiting), focal neurological deficits (depending on location), fever.
- **Diagnosis:** CT/MRI — ring-enhancing lesion with central hypodensity (pus), surrounding oedema.
- **Treatment:** Surgical drainage + prolonged IV antibiotics; treat the primary source.

## 3.9 Central nervous system tumours

### Classification

| Category | Examples | Age | Features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gliomas (from glial cells) | Astrocytoma (grades I–IV), oligodendroglioma, ependymoma | Adults mostly; medulloblastoma in children | Infiltrate brain; most are malignant; WHO grade IV = glioblastoma |
| Meningioma | Meningioma | Middle-aged adults; women > men | Extra-axial (outside brain); compresses brain; benign (grade I most); surgically curable |
| Nerve sheath | Acoustic neuroma (schwannoma of CN VIII) | Adults | Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo; at cerebellopontine angle |
| Embryonal | Medulloblastoma | Children (most common malignant childhood brain tumour) | Posterior fossa (cerebellum); presents with raised ICP, ataxia; radiosensitive |
| Metastatic | From lung, breast, melanoma, colon, kidney | Adults | Most common intracranial tumours overall; often multiple; at grey-white junction |

### Glioblastoma (grade IV astrocytoma)

- Most aggressive primary brain tumour; mean survival under 15 months despite treatment.
- **Morphology:** Marked cellular atypia, necrosis, pseudopalisading cells around necrosis, endothelial proliferation.
- **Features:** Rapidly progressive headache, raised ICP, focal deficits, seizures.
- **Treatment:** Maximum safe surgical resection + radiotherapy + temozolomide.

### Common features of CNS tumours (all types)

1. **Raised ICP:** Headache (worst in the morning), projectile vomiting, papilloedema.
2. **Focal deficits:** Depend on location — frontal (personality change, hemiparesis), temporal (memory, aphasia), parietal (sensory, spatial neglect), occipital (visual), cerebellum (ataxia, nystagmus), spinal cord (paraplegia, sensory level).
3. **Seizures:** Partial or generalised; first adult-onset seizure needs brain imaging.

**Nursing care for CNS tumours:**
- Neurological observations (GCS, pupils, power in all limbs).
- Dexamethasone as ordered for perioeudema; proton pump inhibitor (gastric protection from steroids).
- Seizure precautions (padded cot sides, suction, oxygen).
- Pre-operative craniotomy care: consent, hair removal, IV access, bowel preparation.
- Post-operative craniotomy care: hourly GCS and pupils; head-of-bed elevation 30°; watch for CSF leak (clear fluid from nose or ear — do NOT block it, inform doctor); wound care; physiotherapy for deficits.
- Palliative care planning for high-grade gliomas; communicate honestly with the family; pain and symptom management; emotional and spiritual support.

---

## Remember

- Fibroadenoma = most common benign breast tumour; young women; mobile; not cancer.
- Fibrocystic change = most common benign breast condition; reproductive age; cyclic pain; benign unless atypical hyperplasia.
- Breast carcinoma: BRCA1/2 mutation + other oestrogen-related risk factors; ER/PR status guides hormone therapy; HER2 status guides trastuzumab.
- Mastectomy nursing: no BP or venepuncture ipsilateral arm; arm exercises for lymphoedema; BSE teaching.
- Raised ICP = headache + vomiting + papilloedema; unilateral fixed dilated pupil = herniation emergency.
- Meningococcal meningitis: non-blanching petechial rash + fever + neck stiffness = life-threatening emergency; IV ceftriaxone immediately.
- TB meningitis: basal meningitis, CSF has very low glucose and high protein, lymphocytes; 4-drug anti-TB.
- HSV encephalitis: temporal lobe; treat with IV aciclovir urgently.
- Glioblastoma = most malignant primary brain tumour; medulloblastoma = most common malignant paediatric brain tumour.
- Metastases = most common intracranial tumours overall; from lung and breast most often.

# Unit 4: Clinical pathology — body cavity fluids, semen, urine and faeces

This unit covers laboratory examination of body fluids and excretions. For each specimen, learn: what is normal, how to collect it correctly, and how to interpret common abnormalities. Nurses collect most of these specimens, so technique matters as much as theory.

---

## 4.1 Body cavity fluid examination

### Principles: transudate vs exudate

Whenever fluid accumulates in a cavity (pleural, pericardial, peritoneal), the first question is whether it is a transudate (leaking from intact vessels due to pressure or protein imbalance) or an exudate (leaking from damaged or inflamed vessels).

**Light's criteria** (pleural fluid — any two of three features present = exudate):

| Criterion | Transudate | Exudate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pleural fluid protein / serum protein | < 0.5 | > 0.5 |
| Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH | < 0.6 | > 0.6 |
| Pleural fluid LDH | < ⅔ upper limit of normal serum LDH | > ⅔ upper limit |

| Feature | Transudate | Exudate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specific gravity | < 1.012 | > 1.020 |
| Protein | < 3 g/dL | > 3 g/dL |
| Appearance | Clear, pale yellow | Cloudy, may be bloody or purulent |
| Cells | Few (<1000/µL) | Many (leucocytes, RBCs depending on cause) |
| Glucose | Normal | Low (infection, malignancy) |

### Pleural fluid

- Collected by thoracocentesis (pleural tap).
- **Transudate causes:** Heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia.
- **Exudate causes:** Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), TB (lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein), malignancy (cytology for cancer cells), pulmonary embolism.
- **Additional tests:** Glucose (low in empyema and TB), pH (low in empyema), adenosine deaminase (ADA — raised in TB), Gram stain and culture, cytology for malignant cells.
- **Nursing (thoracocentesis):** Position the patient sitting upright leaning forward on a table (or lateral decubitus); help maintain sterile field; monitor for pneumothorax (sudden dyspnoea, reduced breath sounds) and hypotension; label specimen correctly with time and date.

### Pericardial fluid

- Collected by pericardiocentesis (a cardiologist procedure).
- Causes of pericardial effusion: viral pericarditis (most common), TB, uraemia, malignancy, post-MI.
- Large effusion → cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: raised JVP, low BP, muffled heart sounds).

### Ascites (peritoneal fluid)

- Collected by paracentesis (abdominal tap).
- **Transudate:** Cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, Budd-Chiari syndrome.
- **Exudate:** TB peritonitis, malignant ascites (ovarian, bowel, liver), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
- **SAAG (Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient):** Serum albumin − ascites albumin.
  - SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL → portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure) — transudate mechanism.
  - SAAG < 1.1 g/dL → non-portal hypertension cause (TB, malignancy) — exudate mechanism.
- **Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP):** Complication of cirrhosis; polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) count >250/µL in ascites; treat with cefotaxime IV.
- **Nursing (paracentesis):** Empty bladder first; assist patient in supine or semi-recumbent position; sterile technique; label samples; watch for fluid leak from site, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance after large-volume paracentesis (give albumin infusion as ordered).

---

## 4.2 Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination

CSF is obtained by **lumbar puncture (LP)** between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (below the conus medullaris).

**Contraindications to LP:** Raised ICP with space-occupying lesion (risk of brainstem herniation — always do CT head before LP if focal deficit or papilloedema).

### Normal CSF values

| Parameter | Normal value |
| --- | --- |
| Pressure | 70–180 mmH₂O (measured with patient lying flat) |
| Appearance | Crystal clear, like water |
| Protein | 15–45 mg/dL |
| Glucose | 50–80 mg/dL (or ≥60% of blood glucose) |
| Cells | <5/µL (all mononuclear; no RBCs) |
| Colour | Colourless |

### CSF findings in common meningeal diseases

| Disease | Appearance | Pressure | Cells | Protein | Glucose | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Clear | 70–180 | <5 lymphocytes | 15–45 | 50–80 (≥60% blood) | — |
| Bacterial meningitis | Turbid/purulent | Raised | Hundreds–thousands; neutrophils | High (>100 mg/dL) | Very low (<40) | Gram stain/culture positive |
| Viral meningitis | Clear | Normal or mildly raised | Tens–hundreds; lymphocytes | Mildly raised | Normal or mildly low | PCR for virus |
| TB meningitis | Clear or slightly yellow | Raised | Tens–hundreds; lymphocytes | Very high (>200) | Very low | AFB smear/culture; fibrin web; ADA raised |
| Subarachnoid haemorrhage | Uniformly blood-stained → xanthochromic (yellow) after centrifugation | Raised | RBCs | High | Normal | Xanthochromia confirms SAH (not traumatic tap) |

**Nursing care post-LP:**
- Lie flat for 2–4 hours to prevent post-LP headache (from low CSF pressure).
- Encourage fluids.
- Monitor for headache (treat with simple analgesia, caffeine; blood patch for severe headache).
- Watch for signs of meningism, neurological deterioration, or infection at puncture site.
- Label all three numbered tubes correctly (cell count is usually from tube 3 to avoid false positive from blood in tube 1).

---

## 4.3 Semen analysis

Semen analysis is the first-line investigation for male infertility. The nurse's role is in correct collection instruction and labelling.

### Collection technique (nurse to teach)

- Abstain from ejaculation for 2–5 days before collection (not less, not more).
- Collect entire sample by masturbation directly into the sterile container provided.
- Collect at home or in a private room at the lab; deliver within 30–60 minutes; keep the container at body temperature (inside clothing) during transport.
- Label with name, date, time of collection, days of abstinence.

### WHO 2021 reference values (lower reference limits)

| Parameter | Lower reference limit |
| --- | --- |
| Volume | ≥ 1.4 mL |
| Total sperm count | ≥ 39 million |
| Sperm concentration | ≥ 16 million/mL |
| Total motility (progressive + non-progressive) | ≥ 42% |
| Progressive motility | ≥ 30% |
| Morphology (strict Kruger criteria) | ≥ 4% normal forms |

### Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Azoospermia | No sperm (obstructive or non-obstructive) |
| Oligospermia | Low sperm count |
| Asthenospermia | Poor motility |
| Teratospermia | Abnormal morphology |
| Oligoasthenoteratospermia (OAT) | All three abnormal |

**Nursing:** Use non-judgmental communication; explain the procedure privately; ensure the patient understands the significance of proper collection (incomplete samples or time delay give false results).

---

## 4.4 Urinalysis

A complete urinalysis has three parts: macroscopic (visual), dipstick (chemical), and microscopic.

### Macroscopic

| Colour/appearance | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| Pale yellow, clear | Normal |
| Dark yellow/amber | Concentrated urine; dehydration |
| Red/brown | Haematuria (RBCs), haemoglobinuria (haemolysis), myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) |
| Cloudy | Pyuria (pus), phosphaturia, chyluria |
| Frothy | Proteinuria |
| Foamy orange-yellow | Bilirubinuria (obstructive jaundice) |

### Dipstick (chemical)

| Parameter | Normal | Abnormal and significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH | 4.5–8.0 | Acid in ketoacidosis; alkaline in UTI (urea-splitting bacteria) |
| Specific gravity (SG) | 1.001–1.035 | Fixed 1.010 = poor renal concentrating ability (CKD) |
| Protein | Negative (trace allowed) | 1+ or more = proteinuria; always measure 24-h urine protein to quantify |
| Glucose | Negative | Glycosuria: diabetes mellitus, Fanconi syndrome |
| Ketones | Negative | Diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation |
| Bilirubin | Negative | Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia — obstructive jaundice |
| Urobilinogen | Small amount | Raised in hepatic or haemolytic jaundice; absent in complete biliary obstruction |
| Blood | Negative | 1+ or more = haematuria or haemoglobinuria |
| Nitrites | Negative | Positive = nitrate-reducing bacteria (Gram-negative UTI — E. coli) |
| Leucocyte esterase | Negative | Positive = pyuria (UTI) |

### Microscopic (urine sediment)

| Finding | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| RBCs | Haematuria: GN (dysmorphic RBCs), cystitis, stone, tumour |
| WBCs / pus cells | UTI, interstitial nephritis; >5 WBCs/HPF is abnormal |
| Bacteria | UTI (send for culture/sensitivity) |
| Hyaline casts | Normal in small numbers; dehydration, strenuous exercise |
| Granular casts | ATN, GN |
| RBC casts | Glomerulonephritis (pathognomonic) |
| WBC casts | Pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis |
| Waxy/broad casts | Advanced CKD (dilated tubules) |
| Fatty casts / oval fat bodies | Nephrotic syndrome |
| Crystals | Uric acid (gout, uric acid stones), calcium oxalate (hyperoxaluria, some stones) |

### 24-hour urine protein and creatinine clearance

- **24-h urine protein:** Quantifies proteinuria; >3.5 g/day = nephrotic range.
- **Creatinine clearance (mL/min) = (Urinary creatinine × Urine volume) ÷ Serum creatinine** — estimates GFR.
- **Spot urine protein : creatinine ratio** can be used instead of 24-h collection (ratio >3.5 ≈ nephrotic range proteinuria).

**Nursing — urine collection:**
- Mid-stream urine (MSU) for culture: clean perineum/glans, start to void, then catch mid-stream into sterile container; deliver to lab within 2 hours or refrigerate.
- 24-h urine: discard first morning void, collect all subsequent urine including the next morning void into the large container (keep refrigerated); record total volume and send 20 mL aliquot.
- Catheter specimen of urine (CSU): aspirate from the port on the catheter with a sterile syringe (never from the bag).

---

## 4.5 Faeces examination

### Macroscopic

| Appearance | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| Pale, greasy, bulky | Steatorrhoea — fat malabsorption (chronic pancreatitis, coeliac disease) |
| Tarry black (melaena) | Upper GI bleeding (blood digested during transit) |
| Bright red blood | Lower GI bleeding (rectum, sigmoid, haemorrhoids) |
| Mucus | Dysentery (Amoeba, Shigella), inflammatory bowel disease |
| Rice-water stool | Cholera |

### Microscopy (ova, cysts and trophozoites)

| Organism | Form found | Disease |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entamoeba histolytica | Trophozoites (in acute dysentery, with RBCs), cysts (in chronic carrier) | Amoebic dysentery, liver abscess |
| Giardia lamblia | Cysts (most common), trophozoites | Giardiasis — greasy diarrhoea, bloating |
| Ascaris lumbricoides | Ova | Ascariasis — most common helminth infection worldwide |
| Hookworm (Ancylostoma, Necator) | Ova | Iron-deficiency anaemia from blood loss |
| Trichuris trichiura | Ova | Rectal prolapse in heavy infection |

### Occult blood (FOBT — faecal occult blood test)

- Detects blood in faeces that is not visible to the naked eye.
- **Purpose:** Screening for colorectal cancer (annual FOBT in adults ≥50 years) and upper GI bleeding.
- **Guaiac-based test (gFOBT):** Detects haem; patient must avoid red meat, NSAIDs, vitamin C for 3 days before the test.
- **Immunochemical test (FIT):** Detects human haemoglobin specifically; no dietary restriction; more specific for lower GI bleeding.

### Stool culture

- Indicated for acute diarrhoea lasting >48 hours, bloody diarrhoea, immunocompromised patient, food-handler.
- Common pathogens: Salmonella, Shigella (dysentery), Campylobacter jejuni (most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea in developed countries), Vibrio cholerae (rice-water stool), pathogenic E. coli (ETEC — traveller's diarrhoea; EHEC/O157:H7 — haemolytic uraemic syndrome).
- **Clostridium difficile (C. diff):** Send stool for C. diff toxin (ELISA) in patients who develop diarrhoea after antibiotics; treat with oral metronidazole or vancomycin; contact precautions (alcohol hand rub does NOT kill spores — use soap and water).
- **Rotavirus antigen:** Rapid test for Rotavirus antigen in stool (most common cause of severe gastroenteritis in children under 5); prevented by Rotavirus vaccine.

**Nursing — stool collection:**
- Fresh stool into a clean, dry container; aim for thumb-sized amount (5–10 g) or sufficient quantity as instructed.
- For microscopy and culture: deliver within 2 hours; if delay, use transport medium (Cary-Blair for bacterial culture, PVA fixative for parasites).
- For C. diff: liquid or unformed stool only (formed stool in an asymptomatic patient is not tested).
- Universal precautions; strict hand hygiene after handling.

---

## Remember

- Transudate: low protein, low SG, clear; causes = heart failure, nephrotic, cirrhosis.
- Exudate: high protein, high SG, cloudy; causes = infection, TB, malignancy.
- Light's criteria for pleural fluid: any one of three ratios = exudate.
- SAAG ≥1.1 → portal hypertension (cirrhosis); SAAG <1.1 → TB or malignancy.
- CSF bacterial meningitis: turbid, thousands of neutrophils, very high protein, very low glucose; Gram stain positive.
- CSF viral meningitis: clear, lymphocytes, mild protein rise, normal glucose.
- CSF TB meningitis: clear, lymphocytes, very high protein, very low glucose, AFB.
- Semen: 2–5 days abstinence, deliver within 60 min; normal concentration ≥16 million/mL, progressive motility ≥30%.
- RBC casts = glomerulonephritis (pathognomonic); granular casts = ATN; waxy/broad casts = CKD.
- FOBT screening for colorectal cancer; FIT is more specific, needs no dietary restriction.
- C. diff: after antibiotics → test toxin; soap and water (not alcohol gel) for hand hygiene with spores.

# Unit 5: Genetics — introduction, chromosomes and patterns of inheritance

This unit introduces the molecular and chromosomal basis of inheritance. The genetics module (Units 5–8) is examined separately as Section C of the Semester 4 paper (12 marks). Learn the key terms accurately — genetics questions reward correct use of terminology.

---

## 5.1 DNA, RNA and protein synthesis

### DNA structure

- **DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)** carries the genetic code.
- Double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953): two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound around each other.
- Each strand is a chain of nucleotides: **sugar (deoxyribose) + phosphate group + nitrogenous base**.
- **Base pairing (complementary):** Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T) via 2 hydrogen bonds; Guanine (G) pairs with Cytosine (C) via 3 hydrogen bonds.
- Mnemonic for base pairs: **A–T (Apple Tree) and G–C (Great Couple)**.

```text
DNA double helix (simplified)
5'—A—T—G—C—A—T—G—C—3'
   | | | | | | | |
3'—T—A—C—G—T—A—C—G—5'
Strands run antiparallel (5'→3' and 3'→5')
```

### RNA types

| RNA type | Abbreviation | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Messenger RNA | mRNA | Carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome |
| Transfer RNA | tRNA | Brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome; recognises codons via its anticodon |
| Ribosomal RNA | rRNA | Structural and enzymatic component of ribosomes |

### Protein synthesis

- **Transcription:** DNA → mRNA in the nucleus; RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand (3'→5') and synthesises mRNA (5'→3'); RNA uses Uracil (U) instead of Thymine.
- **Translation:** mRNA → protein at the ribosome in the cytoplasm; codons (triplets of bases on mRNA) are recognised by tRNA anticodons, each carrying a specific amino acid; sequential addition of amino acids builds the polypeptide chain.
- **Genetic code:** 3 bases = 1 codon = 1 amino acid. 64 codons (4³) code for 20 amino acids — the code is **degenerate** (multiple codons for one amino acid). Stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) end translation.

---

## 5.2 Chromosomes and the karyotype

- Humans have **46 chromosomes** in 23 pairs.
  - **22 pairs of autosomes** (non-sex chromosomes): numbered 1–22, largest to smallest.
  - **1 pair of sex chromosomes:** XX (female) or XY (male).
- **Karyotype:** The full set of chromosomes arranged in pairs by size; obtained from cultured cells (blood lymphocytes, amniotic fluid cells, chorion villus); stained with Giemsa (G-banding) to show characteristic banding patterns.
- **Homologous chromosomes:** The two chromosomes of each pair; one from the mother (maternal), one from the father (paternal).

---

## 5.3 Chromosome abnormalities

### Numerical abnormalities (aneuploidy)

**Cause:** Non-disjunction — failure of homologous chromosomes (or sister chromatids) to separate at meiosis I or II → gametes with 24 or 22 chromosomes → trisomy (47 chromosomes) or monosomy (45 chromosomes) in the offspring.

| Syndrome | Chromosome | Incidence | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Down syndrome | Trisomy 21 | 1 in 700 live births | Intellectual disability, flat face, upward-slanting eyes, single palmar crease, small ears, hypotonia, congenital heart defects (ASD, VSD, AVSD), hypothyroidism, early Alzheimer's; risk increases with maternal age |
| Edwards syndrome | Trisomy 18 | 1 in 5,000 | Severe intellectual disability, rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia, cardiac defects; most die within the first year |
| Patau syndrome | Trisomy 13 | 1 in 10,000 | Severe intellectual disability, holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, cardiac defects; most die within weeks |
| Turner syndrome | 45,X (monosomy X) | 1 in 2,500 females | Short stature, webbed neck, wide-carrying angle (cubitus valgus), primary amenorrhoea, streak ovaries (infertility), coarctation of aorta; intelligence normal |
| Klinefelter syndrome | 47,XXY | 1 in 500–1,000 males | Tall, small firm testes, azoospermia (infertility), gynaecomastia, mild intellectual disability; testosterone replacement needed |

**Mnemonic for trisomy numbers:** "Down (21), Edwards (18), Patau (13)" — decreasing number, decreasing viability.

### Polyploidy

- Triploid (3n = 69 chromosomes) — usually from fertilisation by two sperms; almost always lethal; partial hydatidiform mole.

### Structural abnormalities

Caused by chromosome breakage, with incorrect repair:

| Type | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deletion | Loss of a chromosome segment | Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) — high-pitched cat-like cry, intellectual disability |
| Duplication | Extra copy of a segment | |
| Inversion | Segment reversed within the chromosome | Pericentric (includes centromere) or paracentric |
| Translocation | Segment moves to another chromosome | Robertsonian translocation (between 2 acrocentric chromosomes, e.g. 14 and 21): carrier has 45 chromosomes but balanced; offspring risk of trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) = 1 in 3 for maternal carrier |
| Ring chromosome | Ends of a chromosome join | |
| Isochromosome | Duplication of one arm, deletion of the other | i(Xq) in some Turner syndrome; i(17q) in medulloblastoma |

---

## 5.4 Mendelian patterns of inheritance

For single-gene (Mendelian) disorders, the pattern of inheritance depends on whether the gene is on an autosome or the X chromosome, and whether the mutant allele is dominant or recessive.

### Autosomal dominant (AD)

- One abnormal allele is sufficient to cause disease (the mutant allele overrides the normal allele).
- **Pedigree features:** Vertical transmission (every generation affected); each affected parent has a 50% chance of passing the disease to each child; males and females equally affected; a negative family history is possible if the mutation arose de novo.

| Disease | Gene / mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Huntington's disease | HTT gene; CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion; chromosome 4; neurodegeneration in adulthood |
| Neurofibromatosis type 1 | NF1 gene; café-au-lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (iris) |
| Marfan syndrome | FBN1 gene (fibrillin); tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic aneurysm |
| Familial hypercholesterolaemia | LDL receptor mutation; early atherosclerosis |
| Achondroplasia | FGFR3 mutation; disproportionate short stature; most cases are de novo |

### Autosomal recessive (AR)

- Two abnormal alleles are required to cause disease.
- **Pedigree features:** Horizontal transmission (usually one generation affected; parents appear normal but are carriers); each affected child has a 25% chance of disease; each unaffected sibling has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier; consanguinity increases risk; both parents must be carriers.

| Disease | Mutation / mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Cystic fibrosis (CF) | CFTR gene; most common serious AR disease in Europeans; thick mucus, lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency |
| Sickle cell disease | HBB gene (Glu→Val at position 6); sickle-shaped RBCs; vaso-occlusion, haemolytic anaemia; common in Africa and India |
| Phenylketonuria (PKU) | PAH gene; phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; toxic phenylalanine accumulates → intellectual disability; detected by newborn screening |
| Thalassaemia | Alpha or beta globin chain mutations; common in India, the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia |
| Alkaptonuria | Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency; urine darkens on standing |
| Albinism | Tyrosinase deficiency; absence of melanin |

### X-linked recessive (XLR)

- Mutation on the X chromosome; recessive — females are usually carriers (one normal X); males are affected (only one X, so the mutation is expressed).
- **Pedigree features:** Males predominantly affected; females are carriers; no father-to-son transmission (sons receive Y from father); carrier mother has 50% affected sons and 50% carrier daughters; affected father → all daughters are carriers, all sons are unaffected.

| Disease | Gene / features |
| --- | --- |
| Haemophilia A | Factor VIII deficiency; joint and muscle bleeding; treat with recombinant Factor VIII |
| Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) | Factor IX deficiency; similar to A; treat with Factor IX |
| Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) | Dystrophin gene (largest human gene); progressive muscle weakness, Gowers' sign (using hands to walk up the legs from the floor), pseudohypertrophy of calves, wheelchair bound by teens, cardiomyopathy |
| G6PD deficiency | Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; haemolytic anaemia triggered by oxidant stress (fava beans, primaquine, dapsone); very common in India and Africa |
| Red-green colour blindness | OPN1LW/OPN1MW; most common X-linked condition |

### X-linked dominant (XLD)

- Females are more often affected (some have milder disease due to X-inactivation).
- Affected father passes the condition to all daughters but no sons.
- Example: Vitamin D-resistant rickets (hypophosphataemia), Rett syndrome, Fragile X syndrome (technically XLD with anticipation).

### Mitochondrial inheritance

- Mitochondria have their own circular DNA (16,569 base pairs; 37 genes).
- **All children of an affected mother inherit the condition** (since mitochondria come only from the egg, not the sperm).
- Affected fathers do not pass the condition to any children.
- **Heteroplasmy:** Variable mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA → variable clinical expression.
- Examples: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes), MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibres), Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON).

---

## 5.5 Comparison of inheritance patterns

| Feature | Autosomal dominant | Autosomal recessive | X-linked recessive | Mitochondrial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generations | Every generation (vertical) | Usually one (horizontal) | Skips generations | Every generation from mother |
| Sex affected | M and F equally | M and F equally | Males predominantly | M and F (from mother) |
| Parents usually | One affected | Both carriers | Mother carrier | Mother affected |
| Recurrence risk (each child) | 50% | 25% | 50% of sons affected | All children of affected mother |
| Consanguinity increase risk? | No | Yes | No | No |

---

## Remember

- DNA base pairs: A with T, G with C. RNA uses U instead of T.
- 46 chromosomes = 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
- Non-disjunction → aneuploidy. Down = trisomy 21; Edwards = trisomy 18; Patau = trisomy 13; Turner = 45,X; Klinefelter = 47,XXY.
- Robertsonian translocation (14;21) → familial Down syndrome carrier (45 chromosomes, balanced).
- Cri-du-chat = 5p deletion.
- Autosomal dominant: 50% risk per child, one parent affected, vertical pattern.
- Autosomal recessive: 25% affected, 50% carrier; both parents carriers; consanguinity increases risk.
- X-linked recessive: males affected; mothers are carriers; no father-to-son transmission.
- Mitochondrial: all children of an affected mother are affected; father does not transmit.
