# Unit 6: Genetics — maternal, prenatal and genetic influences on defects and diseases

This unit extends inheritance into more complex topics: multifactorial disease, teratogens, genomic imprinting, repeat expansions, cancer genetics, and epigenetics — all with significant clinical and nursing relevance.

---

## 6.1 Multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance

Most common diseases are **not** caused by a single gene defect. Instead they result from the combined effect of many genes (polygenic) interacting with environmental triggers.

### Key concepts

- **Heritability:** The proportion of disease risk attributable to genetic factors (not 100% genetic, not 100% environmental).
- **Threshold model:** Disease appears when genetic susceptibility + environmental triggers exceed a threshold.
- **Recurrence risk:** Unlike Mendelian disease, recurrence risk in multifactorial disease is not a fixed fraction. It is typically the **square root of the population prevalence** (empirical risk from family studies) and rises if: more family members are affected, the index patient is severely affected, the index patient is from the less commonly affected sex.

| Condition | Approximate heritability | Environmental triggers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleft lip and palate | ~75% | Folate deficiency, anti-epileptics, smoking |
| Neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) | 60–70% | Folate deficiency; prevent with 400 µg/day periconceptional folic acid |
| Congenital heart defects (CHD) | Variable | Rubella, diabetes in pregnancy, drugs, alcohol |
| Type 2 diabetes | ~40–80% | Obesity, sedentary lifestyle, high-calorie diet |
| Hypertension | ~50% | Sodium intake, obesity, stress |
| Schizophrenia | ~80% | Perinatal brain injury, cannabis use |
| Hirschsprung disease | Variable | More common in boys; RET gene variants |

**Nursing relevance:** Counsel mothers about folic acid supplementation before and during the first trimester; explain that risk is increased for siblings but not Mendelian; support families without overstating unavoidability.

---

## 6.2 Teratogenesis

A **teratogen** is any agent that causes a structural or functional abnormality in a developing embryo or foetus.

### Critical periods

- **Weeks 2–8 (organogenesis):** Period of greatest susceptibility; major structural malformations arise from teratogen exposure in this window.
- **Week 1:** "All-or-nothing" period (before implantation) — teratogen either kills the embryo or has no effect.
- **After week 8 (foetal period):** Structural organs formed; teratogen exposure now mainly affects growth, CNS maturation, and functional development.

### Key teratogens

| Teratogen | Defect caused |
| --- | --- |
| Thalidomide (sedative, used 1950s–60s) | Limb defects (phocomelia — seal limbs), ear defects, cardiac defects |
| Rubella virus (first trimester) | Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (congenital rubella syndrome) |
| Alcohol (ethanol) | Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD): short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, growth restriction, intellectual disability — the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide |
| Valproic acid (sodium valproate) | Neural tube defects (↑ risk ~20×), cardiac defects, facial abnormalities; supplement with high-dose folic acid if unavoidable |
| Isotretinoin (vitamin A derivative for acne) | CNS defects, ear/face defects, cardiac defects; strict contraception required |
| Warfarin | Warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses in first trimester); CNS haemorrhage (second/third trimester); switch to heparin in pregnancy |
| ACE inhibitors | Foetal renal damage, oligohydramnios, neonatal hypotension |
| Tetracyclines | Discolouration and hypoplasia of deciduous teeth; bone growth inhibition |
| Cytotoxic drugs | Foetal death, malformations |
| Ionising radiation (high dose) | Microcephaly, intellectual disability, leukaemia |

---

## 6.3 Maternal conditions and foetal effects

| Maternal condition | Foetal/neonatal effect |
| --- | --- |
| Diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled) | Macrosomia, congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, neonatal hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress syndrome (premature surfactant delay) |
| Hypothyroidism (untreated) | Cretinism (hypothyroid newborn — intellectual disability, short stature, coarse features) if iodine deficiency; treat mother throughout pregnancy |
| Hypertension (severe) | Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), placental abruption |
| SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) | Neonatal lupus, congenital heart block (from anti-Ro/La antibodies) |

### TORCH infections

TORCH is a convenient acronym for perinatal infections that can cross the placenta or infect during delivery and cause congenital disease.

| Infection | Key features in the neonate |
| --- | --- |
| **T** — Toxoplasma gondii | Chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications (periventricular), hydrocephalus; acquired by eating undercooked meat or handling cat litter |
| **O** — Others (syphilis, hepatitis B, varicella, parvovirus B19) | Congenital syphilis: snuffles, saddle-nose, Hutchinson's teeth, periostitis; Hepatitis B: chronic infection → cirrhosis → HCC; parvovirus B19: hydrops foetalis |
| **R** — Rubella | Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus; prevented by MMR vaccination |
| **C** — Cytomegalovirus (CMV) | Most common intrauterine infection; periventricular calcifications, hearing loss, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae — most asymptomatic at birth |
| **H** — Herpes simplex virus (HSV) | Neonatal herpes from maternal genital HSV-2 during delivery; vesicles, encephalitis, disseminated disease; treat with IV aciclovir; caesarean section if active lesions at term |

**Nursing:** Educate pregnant women about TORCH prevention — cook meat thoroughly, avoid cat litter, complete MMR vaccination before pregnancy, use condoms for HSV-2 prevention, universal hepatitis B vaccination.

---

## 6.4 Genomic imprinting

**Imprinting** = epigenetic silencing of one parental allele so that only the maternal or only the paternal copy is expressed. The imprinting depends on which parent the allele came from, not on its DNA sequence. Loss of the normally expressed copy → disease.

| Region | Paternally expressed (maternal imprint) | Maternally expressed (paternal imprint) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chromosome 15q11-q13 | SNRPN and other genes | UBE3A |

| Syndrome | Mechanism | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prader-Willi syndrome | Loss of paternal expression (paternal deletion 15q11, or maternal uniparental disomy — both chromosome 15s from mother) | Hypotonia in infancy, hyperphagia and obesity in childhood, small hands and feet, intellectual disability, hypogonadism |
| Angelman syndrome | Loss of maternal expression (maternal deletion 15q11, or paternal uniparental disomy) | Happy demeanour ("happy puppet"), seizures, absent speech, ataxia, intellectual disability |

**Mnemonic:** Prader-Willi = **Paternal** deletion (or Paternal contribution missing); Angelman = **Absent** maternal contribution.

---

## 6.5 Trinucleotide repeat expansions

Some genes contain unstable regions of repeated short sequences (triplets). When these expand beyond a threshold, they cause disease. The number of repeats can increase with each generation, causing the disease to appear earlier and more severely — this is called **anticipation**.

| Disease | Repeat | Location | Features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Huntington's disease | CAG (>36 = disease; 36–39 = reduced penetrance; >40 = full penetrance) | HTT exon 1 | Autosomal dominant; involuntary movements (chorea), dementia, psychiatric changes; onset typically 40s–50s; anticipation with paternal transmission |
| Fragile X syndrome | CGG (>200 = full mutation) | FMR1 gene, Xq27 | Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability; large ears, macroorchidism, autism features; X-linked dominant with anticipation |
| Myotonic dystrophy type 1 | CTG expansion | DMPK gene, 19q | Autosomal dominant; myotonia (difficulty relaxing hand), distal muscle weakness, cataracts, cardiomyopathy; anticipation with maternal transmission |
| Friedreich ataxia | GAA expansion | FXN gene | Autosomal recessive; progressive ataxia, cardiomyopathy, diabetes; no anticipation |

---

## 6.6 Mitochondrial disorders

- Caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins.
- mtDNA inheritance is maternal; heteroplasmy → variable expression.
- Organs most affected: those with highest energy demand — brain, muscles, heart, retina.

| Syndrome | Mnemonic / features |
| --- | --- |
| MELAS | Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes; onset in childhood/young adulthood; raised lactate |
| MERRF | Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibres (Ragged Red Fibres on muscle biopsy = hallmark); myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia |
| Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) | Acute or subacute painless bilateral optic nerve degeneration → blindness; young men predominantly (incomplete penetrance) |

---

## 6.7 Cancer genetics — the molecular basis of malignancy

Cancer arises from an accumulation of somatic mutations in genes controlling cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis. Two main classes:

### Tumour suppressor genes (TSGs)

- Normally **inhibit** cell growth; both alleles must be lost for cancer to develop.
- **Knudson's two-hit hypothesis:** In inherited cancer syndromes, one allele is mutant in every cell (germline mutation); the second allele is somatically mutated in the tumour cell → cancer develops earlier with less random chance.

| Gene | Syndrome / cancer |
| --- | --- |
| TP53 | Most commonly mutated gene in human cancer; Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53) |
| BRCA1 / BRCA2 | Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome; also prostate and pancreatic cancer risk |
| APC | Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) → colorectal cancer; loss of APC → Wnt pathway activation |
| RB1 | Retinoblastoma (prototype of two-hit model); osteosarcoma |
| VHL | Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome → renal cell carcinoma, haemangioblastoma |
| MLH1, MSH2 | Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC) → colorectal and endometrial cancer via mismatch repair deficiency |

### Oncogenes

- Normally encode proteins promoting cell growth (proto-oncogenes).
- Gain-of-function mutations → constitutive activation → uncontrolled growth.
- One mutant allele is enough (dominant).

| Oncogene | Cancer |
| --- | --- |
| RAS (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS) | Pancreatic (95% KRAS), lung, colorectal cancer; most common oncogene in human cancer |
| MYC | Burkitt lymphoma (c-Myc overexpression via t(8;14)); small cell lung, neuroblastoma |
| HER2 (ERBB2) | Breast carcinoma (20–25%); amplification → target for trastuzumab |
| BCR-ABL | Philadelphia chromosome — t(9;22) translocation in chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML); constitutively active tyrosine kinase → imatinib (Gleevec) is the targeted therapy |

### Key chromosomal translocations in cancer

| Translocation | Gene fusion | Cancer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| t(9;22) — Philadelphia chromosome | BCR-ABL | CML (90%) |
| t(14;18) | BCL2 overexpression | Follicular lymphoma |
| t(8;14) | MYC-IgH | Burkitt lymphoma |
| t(15;17) | PML-RARα | Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL); treat with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) |

---

## 6.8 Epigenetics

**Epigenetics** = heritable changes in gene expression that are **not** caused by alterations in the DNA sequence itself.

| Mechanism | Description | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DNA methylation | Addition of methyl group to cytosine at CpG sites → gene silencing (methylated promoters are switched off) | Tumour suppressor silencing in cancer; imprinting; X-inactivation |
| Histone modification | Acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation of histone tails → opens (euchromatin) or closes (heterochromatin) chromatin for transcription | Active or inactive gene expression |
| Non-coding RNA (miRNA, siRNA) | Small RNAs silence mRNA post-transcriptionally | Fine-tune gene expression; dysregulated in cancer |

Epigenetic modifications are **reversible** — unlike DNA mutations. This is the basis for epigenetic cancer drugs (demethylating agents like azacitidine; histone deacetylase inhibitors like vorinostat).

---

## Remember

- Multifactorial disease: many genes + environment; empirical recurrence risk; folate supplementation prevents NTD.
- Critical period for teratogens = weeks 2–8 of gestation (organogenesis).
- Thalidomide → phocomelia; rubella → congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, deafness, PDA); alcohol → FASD; valproate → NTD; isotretinoin → CNS + cardiac defects.
- TORCH: Toxoplasma, Others, Rubella, CMV, HSV — learn foetal effect for each.
- Prader-Willi = paternal deletion 15q11; Angelman = maternal deletion 15q11.
- Huntington disease = CAG repeat expansion; anticipation; autosomal dominant.
- Fragile X = most common inherited intellectual disability; CGG repeat on X chromosome.
- TSGs: two-hit model (TP53, BRCA1/2, APC, RB1). Oncogenes: gain-of-function, dominant (RAS, MYC, HER2).
- Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL → CML → imatinib (targeted therapy).
- Epigenetics = DNA methylation + histone modification → reversible gene silencing.

# Unit 7: Genetics — testing in neonates, children, adolescents and adults

This unit covers the clinical application of genetics: newborn screening, prenatal diagnosis, and the management and nursing care of common genetic conditions across the life span.

---

## 7.1 Newborn (neonatal) screening

The goal of newborn screening is to detect treatable conditions **before symptoms appear**, so early treatment can prevent permanent disability.

### Methods

- **Guthrie test (bacterial inhibition assay):** Original method for PKU using heel-prick blood on filter paper; now largely replaced by tandem mass spectrometry.
- **Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS):** One blood spot can screen for >30 conditions simultaneously (amino acid disorders, organic acid disorders, fatty acid oxidation defects).
- **Immunoassays:** For congenital hypothyroidism (TSH) and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (17-OHP).
- **Molecular (DNA-based):** For cystic fibrosis, haemoglobin disorders (sickle cell, thalassaemia).

### Conditions screened in India (National Programme)

India's National Neonatal Screening Programme focuses on a core set:

| Condition | Test | Treatment if detected early |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Congenital hypothyroidism | TSH on heel-prick | Levothyroxine → prevents cretinism (intellectual disability, growth failure) |
| Phenylketonuria (PKU) | Phenylalanine level (MS/MS) | Phenylalanine-free formula + low-Phe diet → prevents intellectual disability |
| Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) | 17-hydroxyprogesterone | Steroids → prevents adrenal crisis and virilisation |
| G6PD deficiency | Enzyme assay | Avoidance of oxidant triggers → prevents haemolytic crises |
| Sickle cell disease / thalassaemia | Haemoglobin electrophoresis or DNA | Early treatment, parental counselling, penicillin prophylaxis |
| Galactosaemia | Galactose enzyme (Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase) | Lactose-free diet → prevents liver failure, intellectual disability |

**Timing:** Blood spot collected at 48–72 hours of life (after feeding to ensure metabolites have risen). A second sample may be taken at 2 weeks.

**What happens if screening is missed:** These conditions cause irreversible damage in the first weeks and months of life — intellectual disability, seizures, organ failure, or death. The investment in screening is justified by the small cost of a heel-prick versus lifelong care for a disabled child.

**Nursing role in newborn screening:**
- Collect the heel-prick sample correctly (warm the heel, use the lateral aspect — never the central heel pad, which risks bone injury).
- Complete the form accurately (name, date, time, gestational age, feeding status).
- Explain to parents why the test is done and when results will come.
- Ensure follow-up is arranged for screen-positive results (screen-positive ≠ diagnosis; confirmatory testing is needed).
- Do not give false reassurance ("it's just a blood test, nothing to worry about") — parents whose child later has the condition need to trust that they were given adequate information.

---

## 7.2 Prenatal diagnosis

Prenatal diagnosis allows detection of chromosomal abnormalities and some single-gene disorders before birth, enabling informed decision-making.

### Combined first trimester screening (CFTS)

- Ultrasound at 11–14 weeks: **nuchal translucency** (NT) measurement (increased NT → risk of Down syndrome, cardiac defects, other chromosomal abnormalities, Turner syndrome, hydrops).
- Maternal serum: free β-hCG and PAPP-A (pregnancy-associated plasma protein A).
- Combined with maternal age → risk estimate (not diagnosis).

### Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)

- **Timing:** 10–13 weeks.
- **Method:** Sample of placental trophoblast via transabdominal or transcervical route.
- **Advantages:** Early diagnosis; result available in 1–2 weeks (karyotype) or 48 h for FISH/QF-PCR.
- **Risk:** 0.5–1% miscarriage (slightly higher than amniocentesis).

### Amniocentesis

- **Timing:** 15–18 weeks (occasionally earlier).
- **Method:** 15–20 mL amniotic fluid aspirated; foetal cells cultured for karyotype.
- **Risk:** Approximately 0.5% (1 in 200) risk of miscarriage.
- **Additional tests from amniotic fluid:** Biochemistry (AFP — raised in NTD), enzyme assays for metabolic disorders, DNA analysis.

### Cell-free foetal DNA (cffDNA / NIPT)

- Foetal DNA fragments circulate in maternal blood from ~10 weeks.
- **Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT/NIPS):** Analyses cffDNA from a maternal blood sample.
- **Detects:** Trisomy 21, 18, 13 with >99% sensitivity; sex chromosome aneuploidies; foetal sex (for X-linked conditions).
- **Limitations:** A screening test (not diagnostic); can be falsely positive if placental mosaicism; cannot detect all chromosomal abnormalities or most single-gene disorders (expanding to some genes, but not yet mainstream).
- Positive NIPT must be confirmed by CVS or amniocentesis before any clinical decision.
- **Foetal sex determination ban:** In India, the **Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act** prohibits sex determination (except for sex-linked disease) and sex-selective abortion. Any clinician found in violation faces imprisonment and loss of registration.

### Nursing role in prenatal testing

- Provide balanced, non-directive information: explain what the test does and does not detect, the risk of the procedure, what a positive result would mean.
- Ensure informed consent is documented.
- Support the woman emotionally before, during and after the procedure.
- Explain that all invasive procedures carry a small risk of pregnancy loss; allow time for questions.
- After amniocentesis: advise rest for 24 hours, avoid heavy lifting, attend if cramping or fluid loss occurs.

---

## 7.3 Genetic conditions presenting in childhood

### Down syndrome (trisomy 21)

- **Features:** Characteristic facial appearance (flat face, upward-slanting eyes, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots on the iris), small ears, protruding tongue, single palmar crease (Simian line), hypotonia at birth, broad hands with short 5th finger (clinodactyly), 2.5-line gap between first and second toes.
- **Associated problems:** Intellectual disability (mild to moderate), congenital heart disease (40–50% — most commonly AV septal defect, VSD, ASD), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, leukaemia (acute megakaryoblastic), Alzheimer's disease (typically 40s–50s), recurrent respiratory infections, hearing and vision problems.
- **Lifespan:** Median >60 years with modern care.
- **Nursing care:**
  - Feed the infant with patience (hypotonia affects suck); positioning, special teats.
  - Cardiac monitoring; arrange echocardiogram.
  - Early intervention (physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy).
  - Education in mainstream or special schools — promote inclusion.
  - Counsel parents without pity; support self-advocacy as the child grows.
  - Annual thyroid function test; hearing and vision screening.
  - Explain Alzheimer's risk to families as the person ages.

### Cystic fibrosis (CF)

- Most common serious autosomal recessive disease in Europeans; also increasingly recognised in India.
- **Gene:** CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane conductance Regulator) on chromosome 7; most common mutation is ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508).
- **Mechanism:** Defective chloride channel → thick viscid mucus in lungs, pancreas, intestine, reproductive tract.
- **Features:**
  - Neonatal: meconium ileus (10%), prolonged jaundice.
  - Recurrent chest infections (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus) → bronchiectasis.
  - Pancreatic insufficiency → malabsorption, steatorrhoea, failure to thrive.
  - Infertility (most males — absent vas deferens; some females).
- **Diagnosis:** Sweat test (sweat chloride >60 mmol/L) + CFTR mutation analysis.
- **Treatment:**
  - Chest physiotherapy (postural drainage) 2× daily; Flutter device; Active Cycle of Breathing.
  - Inhaled DNase (dornase alfa) — thins mucus.
  - Inhaled antibiotics (tobramycin); oral azithromycin (anti-inflammatory).
  - Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with every meal.
  - High-energy, high-fat diet plus fat-soluble vitamins.
  - **CFTR modulators:** Ivacaftor (a potentiator, for specific mutations like G551D) and elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (Trikafta/Kaftrio) for ΔF508 — greatly improve lung function and quality of life; now first-line in eligible patients.
  - Lung transplantation for end-stage disease.
- **Nursing:** Teach physiotherapy technique to parents and patient; explain enzyme dose before meals; infection control (CF patients should not mix — cross-infection risk); emotional support for a chronic progressive disease; genetic counselling for family planning.

### Phenylketonuria (PKU)

- Autosomal recessive; PAH gene mutation → phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine (Phe) accumulates.
- Phe is neurotoxic → intellectual disability, seizures, eczema, musty urine odour (from phenylacetic acid).
- **Detected by newborn screening** — before symptoms appear.
- **Treatment:** Lifelong low-phenylalanine diet (avoid high-protein foods — meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts, regular bread); supplement with phenylalanine-free amino acid formula for protein needs.
- **Maternal PKU:** Women with PKU must maintain strict dietary control before and during pregnancy — high maternal Phe crosses placenta → teratogenic (microcephaly, cardiac defects, intellectual disability in a non-PKU foetus).
- **Nursing:** Explain the diet and its importance lifelong; support adherence in adolescence (teenagers often rebel); connect with dietitian; newborn testing teaches parents the importance of the heel prick.

---

## 7.4 Genetic conditions presenting in adolescence and adulthood

### Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)

- Autosomal dominant; LDL receptor mutation → LDL not cleared → markedly elevated LDL-C.
- **Features:** Tendon xanthomas (especially Achilles, extensor tendons of hands), xanthelasma (around eyes), corneal arcus before age 45; premature coronary artery disease (MI before age 50 in men, 60 in women).
- **Diagnosis:** Fasting lipid profile (LDL-C typically >6 mmol/L in heterozygous); clinical scoring (Simon Broome, Dutch Lipid criteria); genetic testing confirms LDLR/APOB/PCSK9 mutation.
- **Treatment:** High-intensity statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin); if target not met add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab); LDL apheresis for homozygous FH.
- **Cascade testing:** When FH is diagnosed, first-degree relatives should be tested (50% chance of inheriting). Genetic testing from one index case can identify multiple at-risk family members — cost-effective population health strategy.

### Haemochromatosis

- Autosomal recessive; HFE gene mutation (C282Y homozygous is most common); excessive iron absorption → iron deposits in liver, heart, pancreas, joints, skin, pituitary.
- **Features (usually presents in middle age, men earlier than women):** Liver disease → cirrhosis → HCC risk; diabetes mellitus ("bronze diabetes"); cardiomyopathy; arthropathy (metacarpophalangeal joints); skin bronzing; hypogonadism (pituitary iron deposition).
- **Diagnosis:** Serum ferritin raised + transferrin saturation >45%; HFE gene testing; liver biopsy or MRI for iron quantification.
- **Treatment:** Regular **venesection** (phlebotomy) — remove 500 mL blood weekly or fortnightly until ferritin normal; then maintenance venesection; dietary modification (avoid iron supplements and vitamin C with meals); screen first-degree relatives.
- **Nursing:** Explain that venesection is safe and effective; monitor Hb before each session (do not venesect if Hb <11 g/dL); observe for vasovagal reactions; encourage fluid before the procedure.

### Wilson's disease

- Autosomal recessive; ATP7B gene mutation → copper cannot be excreted into bile → accumulates in liver, brain, cornea, kidneys.
- **Features:** Liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, fulminant liver failure); neurological (tremor, dysarthria, dysphagia, personality change, psychiatric symptoms); **Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings** — golden-brown copper deposits at the periphery of the cornea (pathognomonic; seen by slit-lamp).
- **Diagnosis:** Serum caeruloplasmin (low); 24-h urinary copper (raised); liver biopsy (copper quantification); slit-lamp for KF rings.
- **Treatment:** D-penicillamine (chelates copper; side effects — renal, skin, blood); trientine (better tolerated); zinc (blocks intestinal copper absorption — maintenance); liver transplantation for fulminant or end-stage disease.
- **Age of onset:** 5–35 years.

### Huntington's disease (HD)

- Autosomal dominant; HTT gene (chromosome 4); CAG repeat expansion (>36 → disease; >60 → juvenile onset).
- **Features:** Usually onset 40s–50s; chorea (involuntary jerky movements), psychiatric symptoms (depression, irritability, psychosis appear before motor symptoms), dementia; relentlessly progressive; mean survival 15–20 years from onset.
- **Anticipation:** With paternal transmission, the CAG repeat tends to expand → earlier onset in the next generation.
- **Predictive testing:** Available for at-risk individuals before symptoms. This is ethically complex (see Unit 8); the protocol includes pre-test counselling sessions and post-result support; a negative result does not reduce lifetime population risk perception; a positive result means certain future disease.
- **Treatment:** No disease-modifying treatment; tetrabenazine (reduces chorea); antidepressants; antipsychotics; physiotherapy, speech therapy; multidisciplinary palliative approach.
- **Nursing:** Provide safe environment (fall prevention); adapt communication to stage of disease; support family caregivers; explain anticipation; connect to Huntington's Disease Association; discuss advance care planning.

### BRCA1 and BRCA2

- Autosomal dominant tumour suppressor genes; heterozygous mutation → hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) syndrome.
- **Lifetime risk:**
  - BRCA1: breast cancer ~72%; ovarian cancer ~44%.
  - BRCA2: breast cancer ~69%; ovarian cancer ~17%; also male breast cancer, prostate, and pancreatic cancer.
- **Who to test:** Personal/family history of early-onset breast cancer (<50), bilateral breast cancer, male breast cancer, ovarian cancer, two or more close relatives with breast/ovarian cancer, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (higher carrier frequency).
- **Management options for BRCA carriers:** Enhanced surveillance (annual MRI + mammography from age 25–30); risk-reducing mastectomy (reduces breast cancer risk by >90%); risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (after completing family — reduces ovarian risk and also breast cancer risk post-menopausally); chemoprevention (tamoxifen, raloxifene).
- **Cascade testing:** Identify other at-risk family members.
- **Nursing:** Pre-test genetic counselling; support emotionally through the decision to test and after results; explain that a positive test does not mean cancer is present; explain surveillance and management options neutrally; respect the right to know and the right not to know.

---

## 7.5 Comparison: common genetic conditions by age of presentation

| Age group | Condition | Presentation | Key action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neonatal | Congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, CAH, CF | Screening — often asymptomatic at first | Heel-prick screening; early treatment |
| Infancy | Down syndrome, Pompe disease, SMA | Hypotonia, heart defect, feeding difficulty | Cardiac echo; early intervention programme |
| Childhood | Duchenne MD, cystic fibrosis, haemophilia | Gait abnormality, recurrent chest infections, prolonged bleeding | Physiotherapy; enzyme replacement; factor infusions |
| Adolescence | Marfan syndrome, FH, Huntington (family) | Tall stature + cardiac risk; tendon xanthomas; predictive testing decision | Echocardiogram; statins; non-directive counselling |
| Adults | BRCA1/2, haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, HD | Cancer risk assessment, organ failure | Surveillance; venesection; chelation; advance planning |

---

## Remember

- Newborn screening: 48–72 h heel prick; treats congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, CAH, G6PD, CF, galactosaemia before symptoms.
- Collect the heel prick from the lateral heel (not the central pad — risks bone injury).
- Amniocentesis: 15–18 weeks, 0.5% miscarriage risk; CVS: 10–13 weeks, slightly higher risk.
- NIPT (cell-free DNA): non-invasive, >99% detection of trisomies 21/18/13 — a screening test, needs confirmation.
- PCPNDT Act (India): foetal sex determination for sex selection is illegal.
- Down syndrome: flat face, hypotonia, single palmar crease, congenital heart disease (AV septal defect most common); screen thyroid annually.
- CF: sweat test (Cl >60); physiotherapy + enzymes + CFTR modulators (ivacaftor) for eligible patients.
- Haemochromatosis: HFE C282Y; bronze diabetes + cirrhosis + cardiomyopathy; treat with venesection.
- Wilson's disease: Kayser-Fleischer rings (pathognomonic); low caeruloplasmin; treat with D-penicillamine or zinc.
- Huntington disease: CAG repeats; chorea + dementia + psychiatric symptoms; predictive testing requires careful pre- and post-test counselling.
- BRCA1/2: high breast and ovarian cancer risk; test and offer surveillance, risk-reducing surgery, chemoprevention.

# Unit 8: Genetics — genetic services, counselling, legal and ethical issues, and the nurse's role

This final genetics unit focuses on how genetic knowledge is delivered to patients and families, the ethical challenges it raises, and the central role of the nurse throughout.

---

## 8.1 Genetic services in India

### Structure

Genetic services in India are provided at multiple levels:

| Level | Service |
| --- | --- |
| National referral centres | AIIMS New Delhi, PGI Chandigarh, SGPGI Lucknow, NIMHANS Bengaluru — comprehensive genetics including biochemical, cytogenetics, molecular, prenatal, metabolic genetics |
| Regional genetics centres | In each state under the National Health Mission (NHM); chromosomal, biochemical, prenatal diagnosis, counselling |
| District hospitals | Basic counselling, referral; newborn screening collection |
| Primary health centres (PHC) | Referral of suspected genetic cases; newborn screening collection points |

### National programmes

- **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, CVD and Stroke (NPCDCS):** Addresses familial cancer and cardiovascular risk.
- **National Neonatal Screening Programme:** Under NHM; targets congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, G6PD deficiency, CAH and sickle cell disease in high-prevalence regions.
- **Sickle Cell Mission:** Specific programme in tribal and high-prevalence regions — screening, counselling, treatment.
- **PCPNDT Act (Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994, amended 2003):** Prohibits sex determination for sex selection; mandatory registration of all prenatal diagnostic centres; strict penalty for violations.

### Referral pathways

Who should be referred to a clinical genetics service?
- Child with congenital abnormalities or dysmorphic features.
- Developmental delay or intellectual disability — unexplained.
- Positive newborn screening result.
- Two or more miscarriages.
- Family history of genetic condition or early-onset cancer.
- Consanguineous couple planning pregnancy.
- Suspected chromosomal abnormality on prenatal screen.

---

## 8.2 Genetic counselling

### Definition

Genetic counselling is a **communication process** by which individuals and families affected by or at risk of genetic disorders are helped to:
1. Understand the medical facts about the condition.
2. Understand how the condition is inherited and the chance of occurrence or recurrence.
3. Understand the options available for dealing with the risk.
4. Choose the course of action that is appropriate for them in view of their goals and values.
5. Adjust, as well as possible, to living with the condition or at risk of it.

**Key principles:**
- **Non-directive:** The genetic counsellor presents facts and options without telling the client what decision to make. The client's autonomy is paramount.
- **Psycho-educational:** Addresses both cognitive (information) and emotional (distress, adjustment) needs.
- **A process, not a single event:** May span several sessions over months.

### The counselling process

**Step 1 — Establish or confirm the diagnosis**
- Clinical features, family history, investigations (karyotype, molecular, enzyme assays).
- A diagnosis cannot be discussed meaningfully unless it is confirmed.

**Step 2 — Pedigree construction**

Draw a three-generation pedigree using standard symbols:
```text
Standard pedigree symbols:
 □  = Male (unaffected)        ■  = Male (affected)
 ○  = Female (unaffected)      ●  = Female (affected)
 ◯─□  = Mating (couple)
 │   = Line of descent (parent to children)
 ═══  = Consanguinity (double line between related couple)
 □ with /  = Deceased
 ◔  = Carrier (half-filled = carrier female in XLR)
Siblings drawn left to right, oldest first.
```

A three-generation pedigree includes: index patient (the **proband**, shown with an arrow), parents, grandparents, siblings of parents, and siblings and children of the proband. Record names, ages (or year of birth), affected status, and cause of death for deceased members.

**Step 3 — Calculate or estimate recurrence risk**

| Situation | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| Autosomal dominant | 50% for each child of an affected parent |
| Autosomal recessive (both parents carriers) | 25% affected; 50% carrier; 25% unaffected non-carrier |
| X-linked recessive (carrier mother) | 50% of sons affected; 50% of daughters are carriers |
| Down syndrome — trisomy 21 (maternal age 35) | Approximately 1 in 350 |
| Robertsonian translocation 14;21 (maternal carrier) | 10–15% risk of Down syndrome in offspring |
| Multifactorial (NTD, cleft) | 2–5% (approximate; use empirical family data) |

**Step 4 — Discuss options and support decision-making**

Options may include: prenatal diagnosis, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD — test embryos before IVF transfer), adoption, using donor eggs or sperm, surveillance and risk management, preventive treatment, or choosing not to test and accepting the risk.

**Step 5 — Psychological support and follow-up**

Genetic news causes grief, guilt, anxiety, and altered family relationships. Counselling sessions address these. A written summary of the consultation is sent to the client.

---

## 8.3 Recurrence risk communication

Communicating probability is difficult — most people do not think naturally in percentages.

**Relative vs absolute risk:**
- "Three times the population risk" sounds alarming if the population risk is 1 in 1,000 (absolute risk = 3 in 1,000 — still small).
- Use absolute numbers: "1 in 4 of your children is likely to be affected" is clearer than "25% risk."

**What people often misunderstand:**
- A 25% risk does not mean "if the first child is unaffected, the risk is lower next time" — each pregnancy is independent.
- Carrier status is not disease; many carriers are entirely well.
- A positive predictive test for a late-onset condition does not mean disease is present now.

**Nursing application:** When giving information about tests or family risk, use clear language, avoid jargon, check understanding, and avoid inadvertently causing disproportionate anxiety or false reassurance.

---

## 8.4 Special counselling situations

### Late-onset conditions (Huntington's disease, BRCA1/2)

- **Predictive testing** for Huntington's disease: A person at 50% risk (parent affected) can be tested before symptoms appear. ISONG/ACMG protocol requires at minimum two pre-test counselling sessions (spaced apart) and an assessment of psychological readiness; a support person; commitment to post-result support.
- **Right not to know:** A person has an ethical right not to find out their genetic status. If a person at risk declines testing, this must be respected.
- **Third-party implications:** A positive result in one person implies that their relatives are also at risk — the obligation to disclose to family is debated; in most jurisdictions the duty to the patient takes precedence over the duty to warn relatives, but the counsellor should encourage disclosure and may assist.
- **Privacy:** Genetic information must not be disclosed to insurers or employers without explicit consent.

### Carrier testing

- For autosomal recessive conditions (cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia) — identifies individuals who carry one mutant allele and are healthy, but whose children (with another carrier) could be affected.
- **Population screening in India:** Sickle cell carrier screening is offered in high-prevalence states; thalassaemia screening offered in some states; pre-marital screening programmes exist in some communities.
- **Concerns:** Stigma and discrimination if carrier status is widely known; impact on marriage prospects in India; must be voluntary and confidential.

### Consanguinity

- Marriage between individuals who share common ancestors (first cousins most common).
- Increases risk of autosomal recessive conditions because related individuals are more likely to carry the same recessive allele.
- First-cousin marriage approximately doubles the background risk for severe autosomal recessive disease (from about 1–2% in the general population to about 2–4%).
- **Cultural sensitivity in India:** Consanguineous marriages are traditional in certain communities (South India, some Muslim communities); genetic counselling must be respectful and non-judgmental while giving accurate risk information.

### Prenatal diagnosis decisions

- After a positive prenatal diagnosis (e.g. Down syndrome, CF), the couple must decide whether to continue or terminate the pregnancy.
- **MTP Act (Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, amended 2021):** In India, termination is legal up to 24 weeks (20 weeks previously; now 24 weeks for specific categories, with no upper limit for foetal conditions incompatible with life or severe abnormality under a medical board). The decision is personal; the nurse's role is support, not judgment.
- **PCPNDT Act:** Prohibits sex determination and sex-selective termination; prenatal diagnosis is legal only for specified conditions.

---

## 8.5 Legal and ethical issues in genetics

### Genetic privacy

- Genetic information is uniquely personal — it reveals not only a person's own health but that of their biological relatives.
- Concerns: **Insurance discrimination** (insurers using genetic test results to deny cover or raise premiums) and **employment discrimination** (employers discriminating based on predisposition to disease).
- **Genetic Information Non-discrimination Act (GINA, USA):** Prohibits genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment; does not cover life or disability insurance.
- **India:** No specific comprehensive genetic discrimination law yet; legal framework developing. Data protection under IT Act is relevant.

### Ownership of genetic information

- Who owns the genetic information? The patient, the laboratory, the health system?
- When a patient's genetic result has implications for relatives, do relatives have a right to know? Does the clinician have a duty to warn?
- Current consensus: Duty is to the patient; encourage voluntary disclosure to relatives; direct disclosure without consent is not standard practice in most countries.

### Direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetic testing

- Companies (e.g. 23andMe, AncestryDNA) sell at-home genetic tests directly to consumers.
- **Limitations:** Mostly genome-wide association (GWAS) data; designed for ancestry and wellness, not clinical diagnosis; not validated for clinical decision-making; variants of uncertain significance; no genetic counselling.
- **Psychological impact:** People can receive unexpected findings (non-paternity, relatives with same genetic condition, risk estimates for serious diseases) without counselling preparation.
- **Accuracy concerns:** DTC tests may miss pathogenic variants detectable by clinical-grade tests; false reassurance.
- **Nursing response:** When patients bring DTC results to clinic, explain the limitations; refer to clinical genetics for formal testing if clinically indicated.

---

## 8.6 The nurse's role in genetics

The nurse is often the first health professional that a patient or family encounters when a genetic issue arises. The nurse does not replace the geneticist or genetic counsellor — the nurse refers, prepares, supports, and follows up.

### Key nursing responsibilities

| Role | Action |
| --- | --- |
| First point of contact | Recognise genetic red flags; take family history; refer appropriately |
| Preparation | Explain what a genetic consultation involves; collect pedigree information; arrange blood samples or tissue for testing |
| Support during counselling | Sit with the patient; provide emotional support; help recall information afterward; arrange follow-up |
| Education | Explain what a genetic test is and what results mean (not interpreting clinical results, but explaining general process) |
| Confidentiality | Genetic information must not be shared without explicit consent — not with insurers, employers, or even other family members without the patient's permission |
| Follow-up and adherence | Support patients on long-term genetic treatments (e.g. phenylketonuria diet, venesection for haemochromatosis, CF physiotherapy) |

### Recognising genetic red flags (refer to genetics)

- Early-onset disease (much younger than typical onset — e.g. MI at 40 in someone with FH, colon cancer at 30 with Lynch syndrome).
- Bilateral or multifocal disease (bilateral breast cancer, bilateral Wilms tumour — suggests hereditary predisposition).
- Two or more relatives on the same side with the same cancer or unusual condition.
- Unusual ethnic group association (e.g. thalassaemia in an unlikely community).
- Dysmorphic features in a child with developmental delay.
- Consanguineous parents (unusual diagnosis or multiple affected children).
- Two or more miscarriages (possible chromosomal translocation in a parent).

### Cultural sensitivity in India

- **Caste-based genetic diseases:** Certain conditions are prevalent within specific genetic communities (Bunt, Nair, Lohana communities — different thalassaemia mutations; Sickle cell in tribal communities). Screening must be delivered without reinforcing caste stereotypes.
- **Stigma around inherited conditions:** Families may feel guilty or be stigmatised; marriage prospects of a sibling may be affected if a diagnosis is shared. The nurse must balance honesty with sensitivity, and stress that genetic conditions are nobody's fault.
- **Gender dynamics:** Genetic counselling must be delivered to both partners; in patriarchal contexts, ensure the woman has space to understand, ask questions, and have her choices respected.
- **Consanguinity:** As noted above — counsel respectfully, provide accurate information, never moralize.

### Genetic counselling process — the nurse's stage-by-stage role

| Stage | Nurse's action |
| --- | --- |
| Before the appointment | Explain what will happen; ensure correct referral information is available; support the family's decision to attend |
| During the appointment | Be present for emotional support; help summarise what was said; note questions the family did not ask but needed to |
| After the appointment | Provide written information; clarify what was explained; arrange follow-up tests; link to support groups |
| Long term | Monitor adherence to treatment; support psychological adjustment; watch for new concerns as the family situation changes |

---

## Remember

- Genetic counselling = non-directive, psycho-educational, process (not a single event).
- Pedigree: square = male, circle = female, filled = affected, double line = consanguinity, arrow = proband.
- Confirm the diagnosis before discussing recurrence risk.
- Predictive testing for Huntington's: mandatory pre- and post-test counselling sessions; right not to know must be respected.
- PCPNDT Act: sex determination for sex selection is illegal in India.
- MTP Act (amended 2021): termination up to 24 weeks for specific categories; no upper limit for foetal conditions incompatible with life (medical board required).
- Genetic privacy: not for insurers or employers without consent; encourage but do not force disclosure to relatives.
- DTC testing: ancestry / wellness grade; not clinical quality; may need clinical follow-up.
- Nurse's key role: recognise red flags → refer → prepare → support → ensure confidentiality → follow up.
- Cultural sensitivity in India: caste-based prevalence, stigma, consanguinity, gender dynamics — always respectful and non-judgmental.
